MT Wan NELLIE, I notice that a large nun-Ler of fur hats an being worn t.is winter. They ~ze ma,-ki-A at all prices, but the very cheap ones are very easily distinguished, especially alter they have been in use for a little time. I think that nothing looks so seasonable as fur, but the brown variety easily hold's the lead. Many of the skaters I have seen lately wore fur toques, trimmed with choux of tulle and bunches of violets, with occasionally a white camellia or a gardenia or two. One of the prettiest toques had a zable brim, and a crown of gold, and jet-embroidered brown velvet. A large bow of brown tulle, matched exactly to the sable, and another of white tulle, with a large bunch of violets composed the trimming. But while re- membering the furs I must not forget the felts. A hat I saw the other day was of brown with a pretty piece of ribbon drawn around the n the left side of which was a ler, 3 wing I vhite feathers.

Children's dresses are a constant source of trouble, but they are nevertheless interesting. For outdoor wear the bonnet is Ain much worn. Nothing could be more becoming to the fresh little faces framed in bright curls. The lace that trims most of the quaint little, close bonnets is another item in their favour, for there is nothing better adapted to enhance the charm of a pleasing face, whether of child cr adult, than the meshes ot good lace, even the excellent imitkions ; some of them not to be distinguished from the real, exeept on very close examination. Children's party frocks are very interesting garments to design. You should remember that thick ruffles of lace or chiffon worn round the throat are not advisable, as this is one of the pordons of the body where heat is very much felt. Skirts are worn longer by phildren than they have been for some seasons, out many parents still prefer them short, giving freedom to the active little legs. Tan silk stockings and suede shoes to match are in great request, ranking next to white, and looking quite as well. The pale tan openwork stockings are often embroidered with some little blossom in the colour of the dress or its trimmings.

There is a very popular saying that "All is not gold that glitters." Now it occurs to me that if one was to look beneath the surface of some °I the magnificent heads of hair that are to be seen just now, it would not be found that it all belonged to the wearer. Of course that is one of the preroga- tives of the female sex. Beneath the heads of fashionable femininity you would most infallibly discover that, in nine cases out of ten, the beauti- aul roundness of the waved coifurea was due to the inner presence of a hair-frame. Two years ago they made a modest first appearance as a support for the "bun " coil, but now have be- come of the must popular and successful aids to fashionable hairdressirg. They so far improve the hair that you must admire the soft coils and loops, which are in some cases dressed mid-way on the head. These are the becoming waves, and a de- lightful arrangement of loosely waved hair, which, In accordance with a favourite fashion of the moment, is parted at the left side.

I have not said anything lately about needle- work. Here is a pretty cross-stitch pattern. The design is taken from an old sampler of upwards of a hundred different cross-stitch patterns worked in gay-coloured silks on homespim linen. This particular example is suitable for the ornamenta- tion of a small tray-clot or a BO of 12010-platB, and may be worked out in a variety oi waft A pretty tray-olot'n, for instance, might be made of fine white linen with the design worked in ingrain red and blue cottons, or, if something very dainty were desired, the foundation material might be pale blue linen, and the embroidery executed in pink and blue flax- thread or waling filoselles. In the original design three initials occupied the centre, but as they were not, particularly good in shape it was thought advisable to block them out. Nicely-proportioned initials, however, or a simple monogram, might be introduced if the idea is approved of. The beat way of trimming tray. cloths and mats of this description is with a rather narrow lace, through which a few threads of the cotton or flax used for the embroidery have been run; or, as an alternative, the edges may be finished with hem-stitching. There are some magnificent toys for the children to be seen just now, but they are very expensive, although worth the money charged. Perhaps the most popular toyi, of the season are soldiers and all accessories of military encampment. Fancy getting a strong fort, with cannon end regiments of soldiers, surrounded by a moat, full of water, and in it live gold-filh and a mechanical man-of-war, which goes round and round the fort. There are forte with two complete railway systems, with clockwork trains that are constantly in motion. There are railway cuttings, stations, telegraph offices, suspension and other bridges, and the whole is lighted by electricity. There are lamps in the stations, and also tall arc-lamps along the line. If that is not enough to make a young lad's mouth water, I should be glad if you eau Inform _ _
Your loving JENNIE.
THE MOST NUTRITIOUS'.

div.head: CHAPTER XVI.
div.p: CHAPTER XVI.

She walked very slowly and wearily towards the house. It was situated in the middle of the street, and it was just like its neighbours; but she had remembered the number—No. 13—no, she could not forget another number now She reached the house and passed it. She wanted to put off the moment of entering it, and yet it was getting cold, and she was—oh, so tired and unhappy. After all, this Mrs. Scott had not spoken unkindly to her. No other had even offered her help. She passed again, then she retraced her steps. She was suddenly frightened by seeing that a gentleman was walking behind her, and seemed to be following her. She stopped short. She must go into Mrs. Scott to get out of his way. Could it be possible that James Felton had sent him to find her and bring her back to him? She quickly turned towards the house, and went to the steps. At that minute the stranger came up to her, and looking at her, he politely took off his hat.
"Excuse me, are you looking for a house ? " "Yes, Mrs. Scott's house, and I know it is here," she said, coldly. "Do you come by—appointment ? " .._ _ _ . ._

Ruby drew herself 4.- "I do not know why you ask me these questions? I am coming to lodge here." "You come from the country ? " "I have come up for the day," said Ruby, shortly, "but I cannot get back to-night; and this lady told me she let lodgings." Ruby's voice trembled. She would not cry, but she felt as if she could hardly prevent the tears from falling. _ _ _

"I thought so. My dear young lady, I saw you hesitate. You do not look like a town lady. You —may I suggest that you had better not go there." Ruby paused, and looked at the stranger. He had a kind face, but Ruby had now become suspicious. Oh, it was only a trap of that James Felton to get her into his power. That was all. "Thank you, but I left my bag here this morn- ing, and I wish to stay here." "You had better not go to ask for it, if you will let me advise you." "No, thank you," answered Ruby, again getting frightened. "—l—l—" Her voice trembled, and in spite of herself tears ran down her face.

She turned away from him, and began to walk up the stone steps. The gentleman came after her. "1 cannot be mistaken. You are young and unknowing of the ways of this great city. Will you come with me, and I will take you to my mother, and you can write to your friends from there? " "Oh, I have some friends, but I have lost the address; and I was looking for a Mrs. Scott when I came here." Ruby was conquered by the kindness of his voice. "I understand now. Will you trust me? Don't think that I could deceive you." Ruby looked at him for a moment, then with the instinct of a child who knows a friend from a foe, she said, quite humbly : "Do you think that I ought not to go even and fetch my bag ? " "No, not even that. You will not get it unless, you go in; and if you go in there, you will not be allowed to come out again. I could see that you were a stranger. Will you not trust me? " Ruby turned, too weary now to argue further. She followed in silence, still half-distrustful of everyone in this big, dreadful London. Soon they stopped at a house that looked like its fellows. Her companion ran up the steps, and was just going to open the dour with a latch-key, but thought better of it, and rang the bell. A maid opened the door. "Tell Mrs. Murray that a young lady wishes to Bee her."

_ He opened the door of the dining-room, and Ruby entered a lovely room full of beautiful pictures. In another moment there was a soft rustle heard on the stairs. The gentleman went out to meet the lady. Ruby heard, as if in a dream, soft whispers of soft voices ; then the door was pushed open, and a lady came towards her. She had white hair, but she did not look old. Her eyes were dark and soft. She gave but one glance at Ruby. "My dear, what can I do for you ? " Ruby held out her hand; she tried to say some- thing, but the words would not come. Then she seemed to lose consciousness of what was happening to her, for she fainted.

div.head: CHAPTER XVII.
div.p: CHAPTER XVII.

Sir Harry had not slept all night. He paced the hall up and down, reviewing the past as man does but seldom in his life, for the burden which con- science lays on our backs becnmes an oppressive weight which we endure without reflecting upon it more than we can help. But on great occasions we are bidden to lay down the load, and to sort it, and to meditate on its miscellaneous contents. If this and that had not been, then such and such a result would not have followed. Why had he not, for instance, paid the full tax long ago to the Feltons, and so have got rid of them and their claims? But some of these questions had such obvious answer* that even Sir Harry could not find many excuses for himself. Towards morning he felt utterly weary, but the thought of Ruby pre- vented him from resting. Had she slept or had she wept away her night? Why had he been a slave to his affections for her? How could he ever have guessed that his punishment would come through loving her? That was the mystery. This had happened to him against his will. He had loved her—this;trusting, innocent child—e'er since he had come to take her back to England. He who had not loved for years, and had treated love as pure affectation of the foolish. But this miracle had happened. He had loved Ruby, ha loved her now more than anybody except himself. What if he were to go to her now and tell her everything? He paced up and down trying to face this problem. Should he tell her everything, ajid gzt this 1-21,ird,,Pri off is shoulders ? A burden , because he loved her. What strange fate had forced this love upon him? What irony of fate had made her his punishment, and through love? But no, it was impossible. What would she say? She would despise him. Oh, that was not the word! Her love would fly away as morning dew. It would be as if she had never loved him. How could he face that? No, it was impossible; as well let her marry James as that! But how could she bear that?

Thought tired him out at last; he saw there were three hours before it was time for the Feltons to go. Why should he see them? He and Ruby need not go for four hours yet. He must get some rest, so as to be able to go through all that waa to happen that day. He went to his room, and throwing himself on his bed at last, he fell asleep till Rudd knocked loudly at his door.

"Mr. Felton has gone, sir, and Mr. James as well. He left word that you would find him at Hotel Victoria. He will take the rooms, and see that everything is right." "Breakfast must be ready in the hall in half-an- hour, and tell Nancy to see that Miss Ruby does not keep me waiting., " Rudd shuffled off, and Sir Harry hastily dressed himself. But he lingered even when he was ready. He took out a leathern case, in which he put a hundred pounds in notes. "This shall be for herself alone. She must not tell James that she has it. He would rob his own father, and has done it before now, I believe. My poor little girl! What an idiot I am!" Then he opened the door and walked downstairs. Rudd came running to meet him, looking white and scared. "0, Sir Harry! How it can have happened, I don't know! I have just seen Bob, and he left the luggage but never saw her." "Saw who ? " said the squire, not dreaming that the girl he had kept as a prisoner would ever have the courage to defy him. "What do you mean? Speak out." "Nancy is wild, sir; she says she went to bed as usual--" Sir Harry seized the man by the arm. "Speak up, you fool! What has happened? It mill be the worse for you." Rudd was as pale as death. I "It's Miss Ruby, sir. Nancy says--" Sir Harry waited for no more. He flew down- stairs. "Nancy, where is she? You are answerable." Nancy was sobbing. "I never thought she would do such a thing! But I was sleeping, and she must have taken my key and aot away. How could I guess such a thing,

The German Emperor having decided that the new century begins with this year toe Post Office at,Berlin has issued five millions of " Century postcards." The en- terprise seems to have te en a profir,eele one for the State, and still mere prefitatee for the dealers who bought the cards,and sold them an hour liter for five time.;.. their face value. Toe coil/ ctors who bought the cares do not appear however to have made a very good bar- gain, for we are told that the Postmaeter General has ordered some millions more to be printed. The appointment of toe Duke of Connaught to the post recently filled by Lord Roberts, will, in some measure, make up for the want of a Royal Residence in Ireland, of which se much has teen ewe at one time and enother. The duties attached to the office of the Com- mander-in-Chief in Ireland, are as neuce of a social as a military character, and in this respect the Duke will have the assistance of his wife wlei is a popular and accomplished hostess. The Duchi S 3 of Connaught as is wellknown, is a German Princess, tieing the daughter of Prince Frederick Charles, " the Red Prince," one of the ablest of the German Gener tls in the France-Prussian War. Born in 1860, she is not set forty, being ten ye els younger than her husband. She was married in 1879, at the age of 19. She is tall and dignified locking, awe comr s of a right Royal stuck. Duriog the absence of the Duke of Marlborough in Srth Africa. tbe Duchess remains with her two little sons, at Blenheim, and never mere the affeire of an estate left in more capable hands. The Duchess is a thorough business woman, and rules her vast establish- ment with a firmness surprising in one so young. Great changes have taken place at Blenheim eince the Duchess's reign commenced, but much remains yet to be done, ere it reaches its former magnificence. In and about her private apartments, the Duchess's favourite hower abounds, great masses of bright pink geraniums being en evidence everywhere. is is well known,there Is an intimate relation between the weather and crime, and the conduct of grown up people and children. Statibtics prove this beyond dis- pute, but the connection is not always in the direction which appearances would suggest. 'fbus, the favourite time for suicides is during the summer months, arid not, as might be supposed, in the winter, which in many ways, would seem to be much more conducive to the causes of suicide. Other observations show that excep- tionally hot days tend to increase the number of violent assaults by men, and it is usually the cese that the largest number of brutal attacks and murders nowadays occur also in the summer months. Professor Dexter of Colorado has been pursuing simile: investigations with regard to the behaviour of school children. Be finds that the general conduct in tee public echools in New York is at its be3t on cold calm and clear days, and that on dull and muggy onee, boils de- partment and diligence are at their worst. There rs, however, much less in this that is seemingly ceutradic- tory, as the conclusion Professor Dexter arrives at is meetly the experience of those who have anything to do with children. A remarkable 1:14 oircumstvitial story, which feeirm to bear the stamp of truth, aas published the other day by a London paper in reference to the disaster at Amalfi. The narrative comes in the form of a letter from an English visitor to the Italian town, and it states that en the night before the landslip, a lady who is de- scribed as " E" woke absolutely possessed with the idea that the roof was falling in and suffocating her. In the morning, as she still felt the same terror, r" E " and the writer left the hotel,and shortly afterwards the building was in great part destroyed. There are many similar stories, but perhaps the best known incident of the kind is that recorded by the grandson of Spencer Perceive', in a biography et that etateunan. Mr. Perceval, as everybody knows, was assassinated in the lobby of the Hntlee of Commons on May llth, 1812, by one John Bellingham. Mr. John Williams. Bart., wrote in reference to the murder the following statement :—"About the 2nd or 3rd May, I dreamed I war in the lobby of the House of Commons, a place well known to me. A small man dressed in a blue coat and white waistcoat entered, and immediately I eaw a person whom I had observed on my first entrarice, dressea in a snuff coloured coat with yellow metal huttons,take a pistol from his coat, and present it at the little man above mentioned. The pistol was cEccoarged and the ball entered under the left breast of the pet sea at whom it was directed. I saw bloi-d issue from the place where the ball had struck him, his ceuntienance ireitantly altered and he fell to the ground. Upon inquiry who the sufferer might be, I was informed that he Was the Chancellor. I further saw the muiderer laid hold of by several gentlemen who were in the room. Upon waking I told the particulars to my wife. She tie aced the matter lightly, t was only a dream."
WO ILJ L.'

Williams says he dreamt the same thing three times, and thought seriously of going to London that he might warn Mr. Percival of impending danger. After however, he had stated to his friends the particulars of the dream and his own feeling in regard to it, they dissuaded him from his purpose saying lie might expose himself to contempt or vexation, or be taken up as a lunatic. It is difficult to find an ordinary explanation for these dreams and presentiments, although it does not neces- sarily follow that they are mon than accidental. Some of them are very exact and circumstantial but still it is a fact that there are some people who have presenti- ments of evil nearly every day, so that at any given moment there must be thousands of these ideas in cir- culation. However,here are what appear to be the facts upon which people must put their own interpretation. Fringed crepe de Chine ties are well to the fore still worn in a sailor knot,after being passed round the neck. They give a dainty finish to a frock, and are most useful as a bright note of colour where dull or neutral toilettes are concerned. They are however expensive, and not very economical wear, which is good news for the " ex- clusive "ones only. The high collars which completely cover the neck and reach quite up to the chin may not be a success from the hyganic point of view, but when thoroughly well fitted they are eminently becoming to the tall and slight. Some of the latest specimens slope down at the hack to correspond with the front, and the point is high just at the sides only: Others form a high band all round, but rising somewhat at the back, others again with points at the ears are quite low in front and slope up gradually to form the point, and then set in a high in- verted scallop at the hack. The latter idea is probably the most comfortable, and desirable of all, " MADGE."

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
Sale of the Duke's Dock, Liverpool. Terms of the Agreement.

A copy of the agreement which has been recently entered into between the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany and the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board has been deposited for confirmation by Parliament next session. , Under this agreement the Skip Canal Company,as owners of the property known as the Duke's Dock, at Liverpool agree to sell, and the Mersey Docks Board agree to pur- chase, the whole of this property, which was acquired by the Ship Canal Company as part of the Bridgewater Canals. The price to be paid by the Board to the Com- pany is to be settled by arbitration on the basis of a sale to " a willing purchaser "by " a willing seller," but without, regard to the past or present revenue de- rived by the company from the Duke's Dock, except in so far as the value of the property to the Board may be affect( d by the existing leases, agreements, and tenan- cies. The company undertakes not to make any claim for any disturbance or interference, and it is agreed that the company and the Board shall each bear their own costs of the arbitration, and pay one-half of the costs of the award. The agreement further provides for the appointment of Mr. Robert Vigers, surveyor, of Old Jewry, London, as sole arbitrator.

A well-known Sunday School teicher has told an im- pressive and interesting story to tbe representative of a eewspawr. He has instructed a success- ful class, and his word can be thoroughly relied upon. The young man alluded to is William Field, son of Mr. William Field, of Littledean Hill, Cinderford, Dean Forest. The newspaper representative adds that he has known Mr. Field and hi 3 family for many years,and the teacher in particular. He is a clever and well- educated young man of twenty-three years, employed at one of the largest collieries in the district. Early last year ho was stricken down by an attack of influenza, and other complications super- venirg he was in a very critical condition for some time, and was the subject of much prayer and anxiety on the part of his immediate friends, all of whom are active Christian workers, and also of his fellow teachers I,J the Sunday School at Greenbottom (an off-shoot of lie Baptist Church there), where he had a very success- ful class, being a very faithful and beloved teacher, all of which facts the newspaper writer vouches for. div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY JANUARY 5, 1900.
CROSFIELD'S WORKS.
Public Inspection.

With the commendable object in view of assisting the Mayor's Fund, Messrs. Joseph Crosfielcl and Sons, Limited, decided to make a small charge for admittance to their works on the occasion of the public inspection held on Thursday, Friday and Saturday last week. The innovation which was made two years ago of allowing the public to inspect the works seems to have developed into an annual custom and that the privilege is appreciated is shown by the large numbers who avail themselves of the opportunity of witnessing the interesting operations which are to be seen in progress. One cannot visit Messrs. Cresfield's works without being struck by the variety of the pro- ducts now manufactured. As makers of soap they stand in the foremost rank and their specialities, ranging from the old-fashioned " blue mottled" to the best toilet tablet, find their way to almost ovary corner of the earth. Two of the latest additions to their ex- tensive list of soaps are " Good Judge "and "Gipsy Brown." Not only have Messrs. Croafield's thoroughly established themselves as soap manufacturers but they are making progress in other directions. Their" Rain. bow " blue and soda now command a ready sale and the manufacture of scent is proving a successful venture. The firm is also doing an extensive business in glycerine and chemicals and the latest addition to the list is the manufacture of agricultural lime. These by-products have been introduced on the initiative of Dr. Markel,the managing director, whose scientific knowledge has en• abled him to convert the firm's residuals into marketable corn modities. The decoratione which had been carried out in the works were on somewhat similar lines to those of last e The workroorne of the young women had teen more artistically treated than those occupied by the sterner sex, and it wax. evident that in this work the mere man comes off a very bad second. Passing under the line of flags which stretched across the entrance to the works and havine satisfied the demands of the man at the works lodge, the visitor is introduced to the box room where by means of ingeniously devised machinery boxes are knocked together in a twinkling. The electric light has now been introduced into this department and the work is carried out under the beet possible conditions He e boxes had been arranged in the form of arches and by the introduction of holly and decorativema, terial the men in this corner of the works may be said te have made a brave show. Proceeding to the stamping room, where the soap is stamned with its distinctive title, and prepared for the haaue of the purchassr, the change wss almost as rapid and remarkable as a transforma- tion scene. The large room was festooned with strips of coloured paper, artistically arranged, and in every direction there was decorative material,with show cards of Messrs. Crosfield's specialities introduced. This year visitors were allowed to inspect the soap parroover forty in number and reaching to a height of forty feet from the basement. From the top a good bird's eve view of the works was obtained. Near the pans are the frame rooms where the saponaceous material is hardened and prapared for cutting. After a brief survey of the dry sop room the visitor reaches the cheap toilet de- partment, aud here and there touches of the decorative artist were visible. In the printing and lithographing room; the card-board boxes and wrappers which are familiar to almost every householder receive their due qeantity of se inters ink. Near to is a most attractive looking room where the milling and packing of the first class toilet soaps are accomplished: The air is filled with the Scent nose familiarly known as" Eraemic " and at one corner of the room young women with smil- ing fac.s and nimble fingers were engaged in filling bottles with this agreeable perfume. Decorations had been carried out on an extensive scale in this room. A large Christmas tree filled with many dainty articles heightened the effect. and one black and white artist had drawn a caricature of " Mr. Krueer" and" Miss Kruger in the act of admir- ing a flower. This was a successful parody on the beautiful showcard of Messrs. Crosfield'a advertising their Erasmic toilet soaps. There is an interesting sample room in which the various articles producei ara on view and a fine display they make. The visitor is impressed with the cleanliness of the works and the surroundings of the werkpeople. About thirteen hundred employees are comfortably housed and the work pro- ceeds without the least friction. Progress is to be seem at every yearly visit and it is impossible to predict what the possibilities of the firm will Mho in the course of a ,eve years.

div.head: POWDER AND THE SPARK.
div.p: THE POWDER AND THE SPARK.

Both doctors said the lady would never walk out again, and her condition seemed to justify their opinion. She had lost the power to move. After every big battle thousands of men, more or less crippled, are thrown on the world. But big battles, thank goodness ! are rare; and will be more rare as men become more sensible and civilised.

But there are enemies not to be overthrown by force, and who never sign treaties of peace. One of them is the combination of causes which produces the disease c 111( d rheumatism. Its victims are everywhere, but "specially in countries having variable climates and much wet, fog, and dampness. Take notice, however, that it is not the cold or the wet which directly creates rheumatism. A certain poison in the blood is the primary cause, and the dampness and cold are the incit- iny causes.

In p!amer words : The acid in the blood is like a handful of powder in your pocket, and the dampness is like the Fpirk that explodes it. But what manufactures the acid r Let Lig hear Mrs. Morison'3 at ory, and then try to find out.

" It was in the early part of 1886," she says, " that my health began to give way. At first I merely felt unnaturally weak and tired, without being able to explain it. Then my appetite fell off, and I ate much less than my habit had been ; and after the little I did eat I had a pain around the chest and a sensation in the s'emach as if some living thing were moving there and 'gnawing me; a most horrible feeling it was. " A new thing also (to me) was the nasty bitter taste in the mouth that stayed by me all the time, but was worse in the morning. A sour fluid would rise into my throat and mouth which burned and bit at times as strong vinegar does on the tongue. I spat up a deal of thick phlegm, too, and it was often much lab)ur to cough it loose and get rid of it. "I had four months of this, all the while hoping it would pass away of itself, or that I could find some medicine to cure it. In this I was sadly disappointed, for the complaint fastened upon me closer and harder until by and by I began to have attacks of rheumatism, a malady I never had in my life before. "This went on from bad to worse, until my pear body appeared to be full of it. It broke out worst in the joints, as I had so often seen it in Chem. It took hold of my hands and feet, which got inflamed and hot, so they could hardly bear touching. The pain was ter- rible, and before long I could not stand on my feet, and I had to be put to bed by bands stronger than m;ne.

"Later on I grew to be so bad I had to take to my bed altlgether. I then belonged to the great multitude who are in the world but not of it ; who live but can neit her work nor take pleasure in living. I was per- fectly helpless ; I had no power to turn from one side to the other unaided. "I lost strength until I frequently fainted dead away from sheer weakness. And as for pain, I was never free from it; I did not know what it was to have a minute's real ease. My daughter and a kind neighbour nursed me, and for over a year their task continued; and those who saw me agreed that I was doomed to b a burden on my friends as long as I lived. "During this time the attending doctor gave me mrdicinrs and ordered blisters and embrocations, but none of them had more than a passing effect. Then a second doctor was brought to see me, and both said I I would never walk again.

"One day my neighbour, Mrs. Murphy, said she ice- level Mother Sig el's Syrup would help me, as she knew many like ewes which it had cured. I began taking it, and was soon much better. I felt easier, and food agreed with me. After this, u9ing the Syrup retzularly, I improved, and gained strength rapidly. The rheumatic pains gradually left me, and in a month's time I was able to walk about and go about my housework. Since then I have had no return of the ailment, and have credited my wonderful cure to Mother Seigel's Syrup, for surely nothing else did it. You may publish till case as you please."—Susannah Morison, 9, Gransden Avenue, London-lane, Hackney, Loon, Ene 29, 1899. The source of the poisons in h2r blood which gave Mrison rheumatism was the indigestion which wedt before it. What we have said hundreds of times,
wc ?V again—the fundamental cause of rheumatism is dyspepsia. Cure the' latter and you cure the former. Don't forget this vital fact.

div.head: BOLD-STREET ATESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. Annual Tea Meeting.
div.p: BOLD-STREET ATESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. Annual Tea Meeting.

On Monday evening the annual tea meeting in c3nnec- tion with Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School was held in the schoolroom, whicti had been tastefally decorated for the occasion with flegs, &s. Abo it 150 sat down to an excellent repast,the tables being prssided over by the lady members of the congregatien. Toe following had contributed trays :—Meseacees Bishop, Bodle, Fairhurst, James Parkiason, Cellier, Gandy, Miss Bensoe, Mesdames S G Davey, Taft, Pendlebury, Josiah Carter, Messrs Carter and San, Mrs Barlow, Messrs J B Isaac, John Hartley, illiam Silcock, Mrs R G Henshall, Mr E J Guest, Mrs Alien and Mrs Weaver. After tea, The Rev. Theodore Bishop occupied toe chair, and the attsnclance included the Revs J Gunnell, H G Roberts. and C H Hockea, Ceuncillor Shaw Green, and Messrs J Lingard, S B Stringer, E Lunt, G Bailey, John F Dixon, Nicholson, J Parkinson Fred Pendlebury,George Weaver Bodle, W Hickman, E Plinston, Clegg and Sandford. The proceedings opened with the singing of a hymn and the offering of a prayer. Mr. J. LINGARD (secietary), then read the fello wing report on the WOrE of the Sunday schoce: The commit- , tee wish to state that the number of scholars on the boo k% is 334, against 289 last year, beieg ars increase of 45. The average attendance is 100 in the morning, and 199 in the afternoon. The number of teachers and officers is 37. The average attendance is 12 in the morn - ing, and 24 in the afternoon. About 90 of the scholars have attended the required number of times to merit a prize. Miss Ashdown has been elected our representa- tive to the quarterly meeting. We have about 60 msmbers connected with the Bind of Hops, and a committee of 20, mostly young people, under the leadership ot Mr. Horrocks, who train the children and provide entertainments, &c., and thereby raise money for the carrying on of temperance work. Although few in number, they are enthusiastic and aggressive, and very anxious that temperance principles should be implanted in the minds and hearts of our young people. When we see what terrible havoc the drink traffic is causing in this and other towns, we are bound to come to the conclusion that the efforts of our friends in this department are of great importance. The Band of Hope Committee ask for your sympathy and support. The library has greatly improved during the past twelve months. There are 412 books and 107 readers. The total number of books issued during the year was 1,234, and the average issue of each Sunday was 23. This, compared with last year. shows an increase of 24 readers,27B hooks issued, and of six in the average issue of each Sunday. At the com- mencement of the year a lantera lecture was given by Mr Parkinson, realising £2, wbials was spent in repairing 63 books. Only 12 books have been added during the year, and if the workis to In carried on successfully, a censidera'sle increase in the books must be made as the scholars have read and re-read the boeks at present in stock. Mr Bodle has found it neces- sary to resign his position as librarian, and the committee wish to thank him and Mr. Parkinson for their service l during the year. The juvenile missionary collectors have collected the sum of £l5 lie lid, under the supervision of the Secretary, Mr. G. Ashton. In this branch of the school work the children are taueht t 3 do service for °teem and (apart from the deserving object to which the subscriptions are devoted) needs encouragement from the members of the congregation. The Superintendent (Mr. Nicholson) and Mr. Lunt, the secretary, have attended to their duties regularlseand have put forth every effort to reach a higher standard of excellence in the school during the year. They deserve our warmest thanks for their ser- vices, as do also Mr. Osborne, assistant secretary Mr. Hatch, registrar ; Miss Pigot, Miss Kelly, ' and Mr. Pigot, our organist, and Mr. Weaver, the treasurer. We must acknowledge that our ; position as a school is not by any means trit sfac- tory. Great praise is due to the teachers and officese who attend regularly, but when we take into consideration the splendid building we have at our disposal, and that ' it is in the centre of the town, we ought to ' have a better condition of things at Bold-street. We think there must be some friends here who could render valuable assistance if they could be impressed with the importance of Suncley school work. The Sunday school teacher, who, by example and precept, is influencing a young life and drawing it into the kingdom of Heaven, occupies a position the angels might envy. John Bright, in one of his speeches' said :—" I think the instance of a good man or a eood woman teaching ten or 12 children in a class is an influence forthis world and for the world to come that no man can calculate." There is no field of Christian labour that can yield a brighter crown and earn a warmer " Well-done" when the work is finished. Does not such a work demand our utmost effort and skit ? We appeal for help, and we hope that as the result of this meeting we snail have same volunteers, and that with -extra efforts put forth we shall be able to give a better report next year. (Applause.) An entertainment was then given, an excellent pro- gramme being submitted in which Miss Bodle, Mrs Williams, and Messrs Ford, Fanshaw, Boothroyd and Hipkiss took part. Songs were admirably given by Mrs Williams and Messrs Fanshaw and Griffiths, instru- mental solos by Messrs Ford, Bootbroyd and Elipkiss and recitations by Miss Bodle. Mrs Pendlebury ably accom- panied. At the conclusion, Mr. GEORGE WEAVER proposed a vote of thanks to those who had taken part in the entertainment and the ladies who had assisted at tea. He saicisthey were very grateful to those who entertained them that night.' The gathering was intended primarily to add to the finances of the Sunday School, and he was sure he would, be voicing the thanks of the members of the Committee when he said they were very thankful indeed not only to those who had taken part in the entertainment, but :o the friends who by their presence had tended to ncrease the finances. They would see from the report

which had been read by Mi. Lingard that it was neces- sary that money should be expended in replenishing the library, as the books were now practically exhausted. He could assure them that any Money that was received would be wisely and judiciously expended. Mr. NICHOLSON seconded, and expressed the hope that more friends would come forward ta assist them ia the Sunday School work. Councillor Saaw GREEN supported, and the motion having been heartily carried, the singing of the Doxology concluded the proceedings.

•A STRAWBERRY PICNIC. "The Morning Leader," July 13th, 1898, says : " M,,ssrs. S. Chivers and Sons, the well-known jam and "jelly manufacturers, understand the art of enter- ' tainment no less than the art of jam-making. on "Tuesday they invited a number of Pressmen to a " strawberry picnic at their farm at Histon, Cam- "bridge. The wondering pickers were delighted with " the sight of two-score top-hatted visitors bending "their backs to the willing task of finding large straw- " berries. It is just twenty-five years since Messrs. "Chivers started jam-making. They now have a thou- "sand acres of land under cultivation. and employ, "when busy, eight hundred hands. The jam factory "is within the circle of the fruit fields, and the fruit "can therefore be handled without delay." At the luncheon which followed, a Cambridge Alder- man and J.P. said When he was shown over the "factory a year ago he w*s struck by the healthy ap- " pearance of the employee, the women and girls look- "log well and joyous, so different from the condition •• of things in some factories he had visited." A London manufacturer expreved the opinion that "the root of Messrs. Chivers' success was the high excel- " lence of their goods,which had made their mark in the "commercial world. People who had the goods once

" repeated their orders." - The Official Reporter of the &vat Corn mission on Agriculture, 1895, says :—" Messrs. Chivers factory at Histon is now well-known throughout the country for " the excellence of its manufactures."
Chivers' Gold Medal Jams and Jellies are sold by Grocers wad Stores throughout the Unite,' Kingdom.

STOCKTON HEATH PARISH COUNCIL. The Proposed Warrington and North- wich Light Railway. A meeting of this Council was held in the National i Schoolroom on Monday evening. Mr. Pearson presided and there were also preient Messrs Feirhurr, Mason, C erica, Whitley, with Mr. Bradshaw (clerk). The business of the meeting was the consideration of the proposed Warrington and Northwich light railway. Mr. Scotter the engineer, was present to explain tee sceeme. Messrs Warburton and Westbrook were present as rate- payers. The Clerk had received letters from Mr. George F Milton, cork to the Rural District Council of Runcorn and Mr Reginald Potts, Clerk of the County Council acknowledging the receipt of the Stockton Heath Parish Council's reselution with reference to the construction of the Warrington and Northwich Light Railway. Mr J Charlton Parr wrote stating that he would not fail te emphasise the Council's views as r:presanting the Parish Council. Messrs. Brown, Brown and Murphy, solicitors to the proposed light railway. wrote : "We are in receipt of your letter and the notices enclosed. We think that it is somewhat unfortunate that your Council should lia.ve passed the resolution, a copy of which you have for- warded to us, without having full information before theca. We believe that as a matter of tact each claus. has been adopted by them under a misapprehension as to the actual facts. The engineer will be glad to attend your meeting on the 2nd January." At the outset of the proceedings, the Chairman called upon Mr. Scotter to explain the scheme. In the course of his observations, Mr. Soother said the idea was to cennect, by means of a light railway, Warrington and Northwich, and to have also a suburban Warrington line between the ends of the proposed Virarrington tram- ways down Wilderspool and Knutsford-roads. At an early stage the Warrington Corporatien had a notion of running their tram way along this road, and it was sug- gested that the co +election of the roads and a lino through a portion of Warrington to the seat) of the Ship Canal would be a great advantage. He (Mr. Scatter) therefore added that to the original proposal, which was simply for a main line from Warrington to Northwich. The railway would provide for the carriage of goods as well as passengers. Such roads as were not wide enough for the traffic would be widened. Negotia- tions with the County Council were pending to make the road a first-ches county road, and he believed it would be made 27 feet for the whole distance. The main difficulty in their district was the road, and no de- rision had yet been come to regarding it, because the County Council Surveyor and he had the matter still under discussion- It would be necessary in any case,he understood, before many years, whether a light rail way were constructed or not, to widen the road from- the Ship Canal bridge to Victoria Square. The promo- ters of the light railway proposed to 3oin hands with the County Council, and, by arrangement, contribute a cer- tain portion of the cost of widening the road and mak- ing it a first-class road. There were two bridges in tee district which, of course, everyone knew were old- fashioned, and ens of the first things he did in designing the line was to make arrangements with the engineer of the Bridgewater Canal, and though he was not at liberty to disclose the negotiations, he could say that the Lendonroad bridge would be in all probability taken down, flattened, widened, and a steal bridge substitu- ted for the present stone bridge, vary largely at the pro- moters' expense. The width would be the width of a first-class main road. A somewhat similar alteration would be made at the bridge by the brook. The whole district would be very considerably improved. The present narrow neck of road which existed in Stockton Heath would be done away with in some form or another. The traffic as a rule wouldroe a half hourly service, and possibly during business hours it would be a quarter-hourly service. The Board of Trade would regulate the sp ed Nowhere on the whole route would the speed exceed 15 miles an hour,and prob- ably the running from the Skip Canal to Victoria Square would be reduced to four or probably to one mile an hour. A catcher would be attached to toe cars to previde abso- lutely against accidents. In the case of a child getting in the way the driver would instantly let down the catcher and the child would be picked up as safely as by any person. The conductor would have two brakes and would be able to draw up the train instantly. A diffi- culty would of course be experienced with the Ship Canal bridge, but arrangements were in progress by which an improved system of opening and closing the gates would be established, and a better system of signalling. An objection had been raised to the light railway on the ground that horses would be frightened by it, but he could assure them that such would not be the case with an electric light railway. The Warrington Corporation were quite willing to enter into an agreement with them for mutual running powers, and they would be able to establish a pint circular system around Wilderspoel- road as far as the junction with Knutsford-road. down Knutsford-road, across the canal as far as the Dog and Dart, and around Grappenhall-road to Stockton Heath. That would be a very useful suburban system, and would greatly improve the district. The Chairman : That is so far as passenger traffic is concerned? Mr, Scotter : Yes. The Chairman : Where do you intend to place your depot for goods traffic? Mr. Scatter: The goods will be taken to Warrington or to the banks of the Ship Canal. The exact spot has not yet been decided upon. The company hope to con- nect with the Cheshire Lines. Railway by some system to the east of Warrington. They would have a station just inside Warrington ;in all probability on the banks of the Ship Canal. The Chairman : Is there a light railway worked on similar lines in this country ? Mr. Scotter replied that he could not point to any in existence, but at least half-a-dozen light railways would be opened this year. The Chairman : You appreciate the difficulty of the road between the Ship Canal bridge and Victoria-square. Supposing you get a uniform width of 27 feet of road- way what space would you take up with your tram- lines ? Mr. Scotter: Our waggons would be six feet six Inches wide. Mr: Clarke: But supposing you get a Cheshire Lines waggon or a foreign waggon it would require more than nix feet six inches ? Mr. Scotter: We should have to comply with the Board of Trade restrictions. Mr. Whitley: A load of straw would overhang the truck. Mr. Scotter: There is a standard set of trucks all over the country. The company would not refuse foreign trucks but they would not have to exceed the limitations fixed by the Board of Trick. They could not take a re- frieeratory waggon for instance. The Chairman: Are you under an agreement with the Corporation for the supply of electricity? Mr. Scotter: We are negotiating with them on the subject. Mr. Clarke: There is nothing in the order that you intend to use electricity or tbat you are going to con- nect with the Corporation tramways. . Mr. Scotter reviewed the negotiations which had taken place between the Company and the Corporation. He pointed out that the Corporation refused to allow the Company to construct lines within the Borough but were prepared to construct their own tramways and consent to mutual running powers. Mr. Clarke: It is very strange that the Warrington tramways will stop 9g feet Irons the Borough boundary? Mr. Scotter: The exact place as to where we shall stop is under consideration. Mr. Clarke: Is It your intention to have a terminus on the Stockton Heath side of the Ship Canal? Mr. Scotter: No ; but there will be a shelter or wait- ing-room for passengers. Mr. Whitley: Will the shelter be on the high road? Mr. Scotter: It will be off the highway. The Chairman: You know what an objectionable thing a railway siding is. May we take it from you that there will be none at Stockton Heath? Mr. Scotter: There will be no goods siding at Stockton Heath ; but there will probably be one on the other side of the Ship Canal. In answer to questions about the position of the Mul- berry Tree Inn, Mr Scotter said the company had made ast offer to take it down and erect new premises further back. Mt. Clarke: Do you intend to pay anything to the County Authoritie3 for the great privilege of using the roads of the ratepayers?

Mr. Scatter: I think that is a queslon for the PAri..3h Council to consider. As a Parish Council you hAve really no locus standi in objecting to the proposal. Mr. Clarke : Bat onr.objection will be heard ? . . .

Mr. Sc tter : You will be heard. If a Rural District Council objects it is fatal t 3 the Echeme. div.head: DEATH OF MR. D. W. FINNEY.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. D. W. FINNEY.

Warrington has lost another valuable citiz3n by the d-±ath of Mr. D. W. Finney, who for over thirty- five years was head master of a. Paul's (Heathside) National Scho3ls. The death took place at his residence, The Laurels, 3, Grappenhall-road, Lalch - ford, on Nlonday evening, at 6 o'clock after a brief illness. Se recently as the 19th, ult., Mr. Pinney was present at the annual meeting of the Warring- ton Savings Bank, of which he was a trustee and it is thought that he c3ntracted a chill whilst sitting in a draught. He went out again on the following day,this time for a walk,accelerating his cold,which eventually became so serious that he had to take to his bed. 11.3 was medically attended by Dr. White, but expired at the time stated from congestion of the lungs. The deceased gentleman was 66 years of age, and leaves a widow, one son, and five daughters. His death yew= entirely unexpected by his numerous friends, in fact, very few were aware that he was seriously ill.

Mr. Finney's retirement from his duties a; school master has been a short one. Only four months ago he was the recipient of an illuminated address and a purse of gold from the managers and scholars of the school, on his retiring from the position which he had held since Dezember, 1861. Lord Cross is the only trustee now living, who hela that office when Mr. Finney was appointed, and Mr Robert Davies,the only living original manager. It is estimated that more than 14 000 children have passed through the school since 1864. Mr Finney discharged his duties with great credit to himself, and that the school has prospered under his care is evidenced in the following extract from Mr. Finney's remarks made at the presentation on September 27th : " When I came to Warrington, 35 years ago. the present system of national elementary education may be said to have been still in its infancy, and Warrington with its 30,000 people, like raany other towns, did not appear to have made much progrese. As a matter of fact there were only about four or five elementary schools in the borough,the National, People's College,and Ileathside being th 3 principal. Now the town with its 60,000 souls ilaS a large nuth, ber of schools many of them among the best in the country. (Applatise.) At first the boys, girls and infants at lleathside were educated under one roof at the old school. but as time went on the numbers increased, and e`arn-st eff3rts were sucoessfully made from time to time, as occasion required, to increase the accommoiation. The net result is that at the present moment you have three schools rank- ing among the best in the neighboutlhood, and of which you may well be proud." Mr. Finney always took a prominent part in educational matters and in the teaching profebsion and during his career many changes for the advancement of elementary education have taken place in Warrington. Besides discharging the duties of schoolmaster, he took a great interest in paro- chial affairs generally, and filled various offices in connection with the church, including those of churchwarden and lay-representative to the vestry, while for a considerable period he regularly read the lessons in church. Mr. Finney was also a prominent Freemason, having held high offices for many years. He was connected with the Gilbert Greenall Lodge, of which he had been a member since its formation in April, 1869. The late Sir Gilbert Greenall was installed its first master, and Mr. Finney (W.M. 148) was secretary. The deceased gentleman would have reached the age of 67 years , bad he lived until the 9Ji inst.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.
OLD FOLKS"TREAT.

An event which is always looked forward to with feel- ings of pleasure by the old people residing in the village, is the aged peoples' treat, which is held annually in the Church Room. This rar's treat took place on Tuesday evening, when upwards of a hundred old men and women, their ages ranging from about fifty to eighty- five, partook of an excellent tea, which was greatly appreciated. Amongst those present were the Rev. H. V. Pigot (vicar). Mr. Ruhert Davies, Mr. T. J. Down and Mr Richardson. After the tables had been cleared, a short entertainment was held, the Vicar presiding. During the curse of his remark, the Chairman wished all present "A Happy New Year." Mr. Down also addressed the gathering. An interesting programme was then gone through. The members of the Church Choir, conducted by Mr. Rose. rendered choruses, patriotic songs etc , for which they were deservedly applauded. Mr. Hamlet Houghton exhibited a number of limelight views, relating chiefly to South Africa, and Mr. Alfred Grounds caused endless mirth with his ventriloquial entertainment. Several selections were given on the gramaphone.—Before the conclusion of the proceedings, Mr. Robert Davies proposed a vote of thanks to all who had /misted at the tea and entertainment and to the Vicar for presiding. During the course of his re- marks he said he heard that day to his great regret that that excellent man Mr. Finney,who was formerly school- master at St. Paul's Schools was dead. He had done a , great deal of good in a quiet way. Referring to the war he said the neble way in which the country had res- ponded to the call to arms had been a marvel to every nation in the world. It was the one bright glimmer in this dreadful war. He hoped the war might soon end. The enemy had declared their intention was to drive the British into the sea, but he thought there would have to be a great deal of driving before the Boers drove John Bull into the sea. (Applause. )—Mr. Richardson seconded and the motion was carried with acclamation. The Rev. H. V. Pigot in acknowledging the compli- ment expressed his deep regret at tae death of Mr. Finney. It had taken the spirit away from him that day. as in him he had lost a dear old friend. He, Mr. Davies, and Mr. Richardson, bad long heel connected with Mr. Finney, and in that time he had done a very- good work in the town of Warrington and in the neigh- bourhood. They felt the loss very deeply. The proceedings were then brought to a close with the singing of the National Anthem. As each woman left the room she received a mince pie and a packet of tea, and the men were the recipients of tobacco and mince pies.
