div.head: JANUARY sTri, 1900.
div.p: JANUARY sTri, 1900.

CONSCRXPTION has been se t The Decline of a Bugbear. up and ,clothed in the most hideous garments to frighten timid people. For a time it was effective and it was believed that it was inevitable, and there was corresponding alarm. Whether it be near or remote, at the present time, it has ceased to very much alarm. anybody. The patriotic fer- ment everywhere has driven all terror out of men'sl minds. Perhaps it may be said that it has made them incapable of judging of the future. Be thai; as it may, the alarm is subsiding, and in a saner mood the whole question of extending service under arms, voluntary or compulsory, may be ex- amined with care and good sense. Our situation is not that of Germany, as described in the KAISER'S New Year address to the Berlin garrison. In many long years of bitter servitude Go d taught our people to look to itself, and under the pressure of the foot of a proud conqueror our people engendered in itself that most sublime thought, that it is the highest honour to dedicate one's blood and purse to the Fatherland in her armed service." No such animating idea can come to the people of this country, and we believe they are not at all likely to admit the wisdom, necessity, or sublimity of compulsory armed service at all. If necessity arose, there can be little doubt that the country would face it and do its best. Yes, say the alarmists. It is not general service but con- scription we fear, each county having to furnish se many men by a ballot. Why it should be thought that this form of service is more likely than the other is not stated. We may assume that the arguments usually put forward by the other side are intendudto be met—viz., the expan- sion of Empire, the failure of voluntary enlist - ment, the cost of maintaining a large professional army. The greater probability is that the three services which supplement the regular army may be so extended, improved, and popular as to make conscription unnecessary. We ,concede, however, that we shall have to;increase our regular army under any alternative scheme. An army of at least 25,000 men will have to be retained in South Africa after the war is over. The Indian regi- ments will have to return, and there will have to be heavy recruiting to make good our losses. But we contend it may be wiser to increase the army on its present lines, and to make the auxiliary forces more popular, than to have recourse to conscription. If this condition be not granted to a moderate scheme, then the country will drift, and it will not be to conscription, but to obligatory Teneral service. A strong desire to avoid that plan animates the best thinkers of the time outside the military profession. The way to steer clear of com- plications is for the State to remove all known hindrances to the auxiliary services, ani to enact that every young man shall serve a short time and become a competent person either in the Militia, the Volunteers, or the Yeomanry. We do not believe that for many long years to come it will be necessary to go beyond this point. It will be answered that a good many persons are not educa- lcated into going as far as this. We firmly believe that this is a true statement of affairs. It must be so in a good many cases, for reasons of religious and political conviction. Bat what we hold strongly is—that this class has been lessening of late, and that the net moral result of the stir amongst the Volunteers and the Yeomanry will be to make those services more popular, and to im- press the people with the added power some ex- tension of the present system would give us in a time of emergency. The general attitude of the Power a towards this country hardly prefigures a condition of peace and repose.
THE formation of an Ex- Labour and ecutive Committee repre- Parliament.

suiting allLabour organis- ations is the project designed to prevent the curious conflicts which end in the waste of Labour votes and the non-election of Labour M.P.'s. The present scheme has defects. Very often the candi- date is sent down, and not selected on the spot. He does not represent the views of the majority of the wage-earners in the district for which he is a candidate. He even flouts the opinions of a large number of the working classes. He opposes the party which has secured several members of the House of Conarnonsfin the interests of the working classes. No question of chance enters into the candidature, and sometimes it is designed to draw away votes from the more popular of the two other candidates, because there is not the faintest pos- sibility of anything else happening. That is,there is no fair calculation of probabilities,and there is a

wantoness of attack which enrages and confuses the minds of many well-wishers to the direct representation of labour. If the Ministry and the majority which are being so severely found fault with for the South African situation had been changed by a fair contest in 1895, other things might have happened. Some persons have calm-, lated that Socialist candidatures and voting made the Unionists a present of at least twenty seats at the General Election. Has labour been any the better represented by these pyrotechnical dis.. plays? Has the cause of Socialism been ad- vanced ? The answer must be in the negative. Where Socialism only means an attack on the Liberals, it is exasperating to the Liberals, help. ful to the Conservatives, but in no way beneficial to the Socialists. There is not now a single Socialist Labour M.P. in the House of Commons. That fact alone is the best condemnation of the tactics which have been followed. Money has been spent and time and votes have been wasted. Any plan that will avert these evils is worthy of support. A central body, making inquiries and consulted alike by constituencies and candidates, would seem to be suited to the necessities of the case. If it represents a coin. promise and a sincere desire to obtain direct representation it will probably achieve some strik. ing successes. By ,compromise we mean that con- cessions must be made on either side, by voters who are not Socialists and by Socialist candidates and voters. So'cialism is only one theory of labour's possible condition. TherL. are several other working theories in existence;; .4tid they de- serve to be respected. In other words the candi- date likely to be mest suitable will be Socialistic and not acridly and solely a Socialist. Shutting out the former and bringing the latter in with bands a..xl banners has produced the present un-.. satisfactory state of Labour representation. The German model has been followed, and not the French model or the American and Australian model. Who will do best for labour as it is? should le the question, rather than—Who best. represents' the extreme view of the philosophic labour ideal? Numbers of working men voters will not have the Socialist leaders at any price. They have tried all round the country, and they have been rejected again and again. The reason is obvious. They would not represent the views of abour as a whole, in any practicdble working fashion and for any immediate gain.

Medical literature will be enriched next year by several important volumes on battle surgery. The distinguished surgeons at the front are said to be primed already with remarkable facts about the wounds inflicted by modern weapons, and about new operations which in hopeless cases they have dared to venture upon. The war cannot fail to have a vital influence upon surgery. Operations which have only been performed in theory have become possible in fact, and most of these risky experiments are understood to have been crowned with astonishing success. Ultimately, therefore, the war is likely to be valuable to humanity in a special and important sense, and it might be made more valuable still if the Government would put the army medical service upon a respectable and respected basis in point of pay and rank. Exist- ing conditions do not tempt men who are eager to make a name in their profession. The men who join this branch of their profession have no ambi- tion to make discoveries or to utilise their oppor- tunities that way. Special exertion is discour- aged. The pecuniary rewards of the Army medica/ service are paltry in the extreme; social rewards do not exist at all. If the authorities behaved better in the matter of fees, and officers better int the matter of comradeship, a new spirit would quickly make itself felt.

Who readsProllope or Beaconsfield now ? The question is an interesting one,because their works are consparatively recent, and were nearly all published within the experience of people alive to. day. Few men have made larger incomes as novelists than did Troilope in his day,and few have been more in favour personally. Then, many of us can remember the excitement which was produced by the late Tory Premier's descriptions of London society under a veil. The characters in several of his novels were said to be identiflable,and, anyway the books were brilliant pictures of society. They were epigrammatic, but they were something more than that, they presented living men and women; whereas the epigrammatic novels of recent years have a- teadency to rely on paradox for their strength and care very little about the flesh tints, or the idiosyncrasies of the people. As for Trollope, " Barchoster Towers" was remarkable for the easy and entertaining manner in which the conversation went. It was written by a man of leisure and culture for people of leisure and culture. There was no panting and striving after effect,such as is seen in some of stir younger fictionists. Yet Mrs. Proudie can never be forgotten by those who have read of her, and the Rev. Mr. Slope is nearly as life-like. Trollope's books had a healthy ten- dency, and no one suffered from headache after them.

More inoculation! Anti-vaccinators have only just begun to enjoy the triumph of the conscien- tious objector,when news comes of another scheme for inoculating humanity. This has been evolved by, French scientists and is designed not as a safe- guard against small-pox but as a cure for drunken- ness. The idea is to inoculate drunkards with a serum extracted from the veins of a horse which has been alcoholised, thereby inspiring patients with "an invincible distaste for spirituous drinks." Such a "cure" does not strike us as being either very promising or very savoury, and we imagine some topers would rather stay drunk than submit themselves to inoculation of this kind. We have no personal sympathy with anti-vaccination, but any further injecting of animal essence strikes us as being rather too much of a good thing. The human race will be developing either horns or hoofs, or both, if the inoculation idea is carried much further.

The members of the South Lancashire Regiment who are at this moment facing the enemy in Natal will shortly have good reason to be thankful for the kindly consideration of Warrington people. Early in the New Year they will be the recipients of a Christmas gift from Warrington consisting of woollen garments which will be as welcome as they are serviceable. The appeal which was issued by the wives of several local military officers has been handsomely responded to and on Friday there was a large display of work at the Town Hall ready for transmission to the regiment. Many who were unable to contribute the garments required for- warded money which has been turned into kind toe the best advantage. Nearly £BO have been spent in purchasing socks, Balaclava caps and body belts, numbering altogether over 1,500 and it is satis- factory to learn that the money expended has been almost subscribed. Farther contributions in kind or money are required in order to complete the requisite number and there seems little eioubt but that they will be forthcoming.

New Year's Day witnessed the advent of the new Shop Assistants' Seats Bill, which provides that "In all rooms of a shop where goods are actually retailed to the public, and where female assistants are employed for the retailing of goods to the pub- lic, the employer carrying on business in such premises shall provide seats behind the counter,or in such other position as may be suitable for the purpose, and such seats shall be in the propor- tion of not less than one seat to every three female assistants employed in each room." Shop-keepers will have to baar this act in mind or ..uiTer the consequences. It will be rather interesting to see what sort of pro- vision is made for the assistants by employers who have to be compelled to be kind. The Act says

that the seats shall be provided in the proportion of one to evety three assistants, but of course, the I proprietor may increase the number if he thinks fit. Probably those who ot look upon the measure as an unwarrantable interference will be more generous than the others in this mat- ter. It is to be hoped that the majority will be thus inclined, for if the letter of the law is strictly •observed the Act will not confer the boon it was intended to. One seat for three assistants seems an idiotic proviso, for the time when these young ladies will want to sit down will be when business is slack, and then all will be equally desir- ous of resting. Much, it is plain, depends on the considerateness of the proprietor.

The death of Mr. D. W. Finney on Tuesday came as a surprise and shoe.k to the majority of people, who had pictured him enjoying the relaxa- tions of a well-earned retirement. That he was not in good health was, of course, known to all who were personally acquainted with Mr. Finney, but no one suspected that his existence was so pre- carious. He was only taken ill on Sunday, and yet the malady from which he suffered took such afirm hold on his weakened system that death supervened within three days. We, in common with all who knew him, are exceedingly sorry to lose Mr. Finney, who was ever a quiet, unassuming, and most genial man. It is sad to think that after a lifetime of arduous toil, he should only live to enjoy the retirement he so well deserved for a few short months. One sees a similarity in Mr. Finney's case with that of other gentlemen who have relinquished the reigns of office with honour only to sink to the grave pre- maturely. Whether the lack of the stimulant provided by daily toil has an enervating effect on the brain and nervous system we do not know, but it is both sad and singular that so many men should retire from active duty and then die before they have had an opportunity of appreciating beneficially the rest and seclusion they have earned.
LIVERPOOL, ST. HELENS, AND SOUT:-I LANCASHIRE RAILWAY.

Opening of the New Line. The new line between Lowton St. Mary's and St. Helens was formally opened on Tuesday, and pas- senger traffic begun on Wednesday. The eight miles of line between Lowton St. Mary's and St. Helens is part of a schsme for which powers were obtained in 1885 and 1886. It was also intended to make a new line, ten miles long, connecting St. Helens with Liverpool, but the powers obtained for this purpose have been allowed to lapse. The idea, however, has apparently not been given up. Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., the chairman of the Company, said on Tuesday that he believed the line was required by the growing needs of the district, and when a railway or anything else was required in this country it sooner or later came into existence. He was careful, however, to say that this was only his private opinion; he was not speaking as the chairman of the Company. The building of the sec- tion opened on Tuesday was begun inJanuary,lBBB. In July. 1895, a single line was opened from St. Helens to As hton-in-M akerfield, and a double line,for goods and minerals onlysfrom Ashton to Lowton St. Mary's. "The construction of the line," says an official memorandum, "has occupied more than double the length of time that was originally ex- pected; but the difficulties which have had to be contended with, both in regard to the heavy char- acter of the works and the raising of the necessary, capital to carry them out, have been not only ex- ceptional, but such as it was practically impossi- ble for the directors and engineers to foresee when their estimates were made. Happily, however, these difficulties have now been overcome, and by the completion of this enterprise and the opening of the line to the public the important industrial centre of St. Helens will be provided with a second railway in their town, placing the inhabitants in direct communication with the large railway sys- tems in the kingdom, with some of which they have hitherto had no adequate connection,esPecially to important towns in the Midlands." The acw line is to be wrked and maintained by the Great Central Railway Company, and will give St.
- Helens access to the who!e of the Company's system, in- cluding the new extension line to London. _ _

" It is proposed to begin with (we quote again from the official memerancium), " to put on a daily service of six passenger trains each way between St. Helene and Manchester, and a; Sunday service of three trains each way, to accomplish the journey in about forty-five minutes; and it is anticipated that when the reverse curve which the Cheshire Lines Committee are taking powers to construct from the Wigan Junction line to Glazebrook junction West is completed an acceleration of the service may be expected between St. Helens Wigan and Liverpool over the Cheshire Lines system. As seine indication of the future prospects of the line it is worthy of record that the revenue earned from goods and minerel traffic during the period that it has been partially open has shown a steady increase. There is every reason to believe that not only will the inhabitants benefit by the introduction into St. Helens of this rail- way, but that it will before long prove a remunerative investment to those who have embarked their capital in It." Between st. Helens and Lowton St. Mary's the new line passes through Haydock, Ashton-in-Makerfield, and Golborne- The district has a large population and many important works, including the collieries of Messrs. Evans, which alone raise over a million tons of coal in the year. At Haydock Park a s'ation is being made for the convenience of those attending the race meetings there. A great deal of interest was taken in the opening ceremony by the people of the district. A special train, drawn by a decorated engine, left the new station at St. Helens and ran slowly over the line to Lowton St. Mary's. At all stations, and at other points as well, crowds of people were waiting, and che,red the train as it passed through. Returning to St. Helens, the Mayor (Mr. Joseph Beecham) offered a cordial welcome to the chairman and direc- tors of the Company e and then in a few well-chosen sentences Lord Newton declared the line open. It was originally intended that this should be done by Lord Staeley,whose uncle, the late Earl of Derby cut the first sod twelve years ago, but having been appointed on the staff of Lord Roberts for service in South Africa Lord Stanley was unable to be present. After the opening ceremony lunch was provided by the Company in the Town Hall of St. Helens. Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., presided, and the company included Lord Newton,Sir J W Maclure,M.P., Sir William Pollitt, the Mayor of St. Helens, Sir Dangles Fox, Mr Alderman Wilechnie, Mr J Stone, Mr R H Edmondson, Canoe Willink, Mr J Wood, Mr 0 5 Holt, Mr C A Rowlanclson, Mr C T Smith, Mr E Watkin, Mr Et Pollitt, Mr J Rostern, Mr T Parker. jun., Mr C W Neele, Mr W G P Maclure, Mr El S Oppenbeim, Me B Darlington, Mr T Craven, Mr W U Elee. Mr M H Seton-Karr, Mr T Beecham, and Mr H Bibby. Lord Newton proposed "Success to the row line.' He said the line ran through an important coal district, with a rapidly increasing population. He had often wondered why the original line from Liverpool to Man- chester did not take the course over which the new, line had been constructed. It would have done much to de- velop the district, and would have been a greatsourc3 of revenueto the Company. He did not wish to disparage the district through which the old line pasted, but it certainly could not compare iv commercial or industrial importance with that which would be served by the new line. The difficulties in connection with the present en- terprise had proved to be much greater than they anti- cipated. But that was generally the case and need not trouble them now. in view of the fact that they had all been overcome. Up till a recent period St. Helens had been entirely dependent upon one line which justly bore ' the highest reputation. Whether the people of St. Helens were entirely satisfied with the facilities it afforded them he had no opportunity of knowing, but it was perfectly certain they would congratulate them- selves on the possession ofea second line. The district was one of great industrial importance, and he trusted that before long the new line would prove a remunera- tive investment. Mr. Seton-Kare, M.P., respendeJ to the toast. He said he firmly believed the.line would pay. It bad cer- tainly cost more than was anticipated at first; but, as Lord Newton had said, that was the case with most undertakings of any magnitude. There had been heavier work to do in the way of bridges and cuttings than was expected,and there were other matters which bad helped to increase the cost. Speaking entirely on his own responsibility, he expressed the confident belief that the Liverpool section of the line would be undertaken sooner or later. The growing needs of the district required a new connection with Liverpool and when a thing was really required in a country like this it always came into existence sooner or later. The train service with which the new line was to be opened was purely experi- mental. If the public made it clear that they needed more trains they would get them. Sir J. W. Maelore. M.P., proposed "The town ard trade of St. Helens," to which Mr. Alderman M'Keehnie responded. Sir William Pollitt proposed the health of the Mayor, acknowledging the great services Mr. Beecham had rendered to the Company. The Mayor replied and proposed the health of the Chairman, who in responding said they were greatly in- debted to Sir Williem Pollitt for the advice and assist- ance he had so freely given to the directors during the construction of the line.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

' "ALL ABOUT SATIN" This is the title of an admirably written article in the "Girl's own Paper "by Miss Christine Handley, MA., daughter of Mr. James Handley, J.P., of Garston and Runcorn. Miss Handley addresses her remarks prin- cipally to her own sex, and is decidedly matter of fact and sensible, giving one the impression she is a practical as well as a theoretical skater. ST. JOHN'S F RESBYTERIAN CHURCH. On New Year's Day, a 'zee party and concert took niece at the above place, which was largely attended. Tea commenced at about 5.30, when hundreds sat down to a capital feast. The Rev T S Morris presided at the after concert, and items were given by Miss Harrop, Mrs Temperley, Miss P Warburton, Messrs J Stubbs, N John- son, John Robinson, W E Smith (Widnes), Master Frei Outhwaite, and a glee party. The procezdings proved highly enjoyable. SCNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS AHNUAL tirATHERING. The Sunday school teachers at the Ruiacorn Parish Church held their social reunion at the National School- room, on Monday, when there was a large number pre- sent. The Rev H B Firth in a short address spoke highly of the work accomplished during the past year, and in- timated the occasion was the 13th anniversary of the Rev Canon Wood's coming to Ruacorn.—The proceed- ings embraced feastings, dancing, and songs. The latter being of the patriotic order provided by Mr Branch. Music for dancing and accmipaniments was kindly pro- vided by Mrs Kay and Mr Tonks.

RUNCORN HARRIERS. Last Saturday the Runcorn Harriers entertained Sacred Hearts, St. Helens, at Runcorn. The visitors were strongly represented, while the home team were without four of their best men. frail was laid over eight miles of heavy country, in the direction of Rock- savage, and then to Sutton Weaver Hall Wood, and home again. A start wai male at half-past three, the pace being taken up by Ray and Hopkins, who made it a hot one throughout. & good race was witnessed for the finish between Ray and Hopkins. of the home team, and Mclntyre of the visitors. The positions of the teams were :—Runcorn : 1, Ray ; 3, Hopkins ;5, Hill; 10. Hamilton ; 11, Clarke; total, 30 points. Sacred Hearts: 2, Mclntyre; 4, Cooke; 6, Richardson ; 7, Cauldwell ; 8, Glover; total 27 pints. Tan RUNCORN BOATING CLUB. - This club held its annual invitation dance an] con- versazione at the Drill Hall, Runcorn. on New Year's Day, when a large and select company was present. The hall which had been beautifully decorated by Messrs. Hitchen and Squire, Liverpool, was tastefully set out with a view to convenience and comfort. The refresh- ments too, were good and ample in addition to being well served. Under such conditions it is needless to say the evening was aduubounded success, and 311 enjoyed themselves thoroughly. Besides dancing there was an exhibition of the " gramaphone " by Mr. Booth, Lord- street, Runcorn ; and a distribution of' bon-bons." The music was provided by a capital band under Mr. T. Knight.Runcorn,while the M. C's were Messrs. W Crosby, R Bennion, F Crimes, and other members of the Boating Club, who did all in their power to secure the comfort •and enjoyment of their guests. The secretarial duties were carried out by Mr. H G Johnson, Halton-road Runcorn.

AFRAID To GO TO THE FROST. On Friday, at the Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. J. Ocklesten, Joseph Rowson, was charged with deserting from the South Lancashire Regiment at Preston, on the 11th inst,—lt appeared from the evidence of P.C. Fry that he visited the residence of the prisoner's mother, No. 4 Back High-street, Runcorn, with reference to another matter, and whilst there he observed a soldier's overcoat. He inquired whe it bsloneed to, and was in- formed by the woman that it was her son's. •Prisoner subsequently cameo downstairs and ordered Fry out of the house The constable, however, insisted on prisoner accempanying him to the police station, and on arriving there a reference to the" Police Gazette" revealed the identity of the prisoner as a deserter from the South Lancashire Regiment. This is the fifth or deb time the prisoner has deserted. He told the magistrates that he I would not be a soldier, as he was afraid that he might be ordered to the front and get shot, Mr. Ockleston remanded the prisoner to await a military escort from Preston. The prisoner's mother is the widow who was to have been married to the man Lambert who commit- ted suicide on Christmas Day. NEW YEAR'S DAY AT THE WORKHOUSE. Dutton Workhouse was en fete on New Year's Day, and through the generosity of Mr. J Taylor, Helsby, tea, bread and butter and cake ad lib took the place of the usual menu. Taking their seats at a well spread board at five o'clock, men, women and children participated in a good" square" meal, not without delicacies either. for tongue and jam in addition to the items mentioned above figured abundantly. After the tables had been cleared, the inmates indulged in a musical evening. The choir sang carols and patriotic songs, " The Absent- Minded Beggar," " Who carries the gun 2" and "The Soldiers of the Queen" being prominent. The boys gave an exhibition of Indian club exer- cises. Instrumental music was provided by the Preston Brook Brass Band who gave several selections. Inmates Price and Shipton gave a couple of recitations which were highly appreciated- Toe smokers amongst the inmates were presented with an ounce of tobacco, extra tea was giveti to the women, and oranges, Ac., were provided for the children so that the treat was complete in every particular.—The chair was occupied by the Master (Mr Joseph Cunnah), and at the conclu- sion a vote of thanks to Mr Taylor was accorded with three hearty cheers. MYSTERIOIIS DROWNING CAsE AT WIDNES. On Friday the body of John Barton, aged 60, better known as " Fish Jack," of 18. Peel-street, Widnes, was found drowned on the shore of the Merseyebetween high and low water mark, by Fred Johnson, of 20,Pitt-street. Deceased lived by himself and carried on business as a greengrocer,and bad been drinking heavily lately. There was no evidence as to how he got in tile water.—An inquest was held .on Monday afternoon, at the Accident Hospital, Widnes, by Mr S Brighouse, on the body of John Barton.—Emma Boyle, 'Ellison-at., sister of the deceased, deposed to identification of the body. He was not a sober man.a,nd was addicted to bouts of drinking.—Mary Melnnery said she lived next door to deceased. Be bad been drinking for about, a month. She gave him a bowl of soup on TueEday.-- John Wall, barman at the Mersey Hotel. Widnes, said deceased came in the house on Wednesday. He was sober in the morning, and he came into the house on Wednesday night and seemed to be very cold. He was there for about a quarter of an hour. He Was not drunk.—By a juror Witness did not see which way he went.—Several of the jurymen said they had seen him en the Tuesday and Wednesday, and he was very cold and ehaking.—P.S. Leigh said they did not find any ready money in the house, but five eld watches. The house was in a wretched conclition.—The Coroner said the police had found a Post Office bank book with £22 to his credit in it.—Fred Johnson, a boy, gave evidence to finding deceased on the banks of the Mersey.--P-C. Turner said he recovered the body. It was opposite the Mersey Hotel about 15 yards from the wall. There were no marks of violence on the body.—P.S. Leigh said they had no suspicion.—The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned."

div.head: BOY'S DANGEROUS ESCAPADE.
div.p: A BOY'S DANGEROUS ESCAPADE.

Riding in a Luggage Train. A remanded case was brought up on Tuesday, before Mr. John Ockleston, when John Newman, 18 years of age, was charged with travellinz on the London and North-Weitern Railway without having paid his fare, and with intent to defraud.—Detective Atkinson, of the Railway Police prosecuted.—lt appeared prisoner and another youth named Clifford were seen to alight from the waggon of a goods train at Haltom Station. on Friday morning. A foremen platelayer pursued them, and. the prisoner was captured and taken back to the station. From a statement made by the misoner to the officials it appeared that he resided at No. 4, Church-way,Somers Town. London. He left home about 6 p.m. on Thursday the 28th of December, with three other boys named Robert Clifford (amonosed to belong to Liver- pool), John Mitchell (Hampstead Heath). and Joseph Keefe who prisoner said. had escaped from Black Friars Hnme, London. Clifford took them to Chalk Farm Station, and said he would take them to Coventry as it as as a better place than London. He promised them all suite of clothes if they would go with him. They all wont on to the railway line, and Clifford and Keefe cut the ropes of a sheet covering a waggon, and they got into it, covering them- selves with the sheet. The waggon was backed into the goods shed,and whilst there a porter came and removed the sheet. He captured Mitchell and Keefe, but the prisoner and Clifford got away. The two latter sub- sequently got into another truck, some distance away, and again covered themselves with a waggon sheet. Prisoner went to sleep,but awoke some time afterwards by the moving of the waggon, which did not stop until Halton Station was reached. The youths then got out of the waggon, and were making off when they were detected by William Kettle, foreman platelayer. He called to the youths to stop, but they would not, and he gave chase and captured the prisoner. The prisoner, it , seems, had only recently made the acquaintance of Clifford. Prisoner admitted having been five years in St. Nicholas' Industrial School, Manor Park, Guilford, haying left there on the 4th March.—lt was suggested that the boy should be sent back to London but Detective Atkinson intimated the railway authorities would not do that. —Prisoner was therefore remanded to Monday next, so that the Railway Police might cemplete their inepiries concerning the other boys spoken about by the prisoner.

The number in the corrsiannlincx five weeks of 1893 was 385 showing a riecreabe of 12, he:ng a net decrease in 1899, to date, of 190.
RUNCORN BOARD OF
GUARDIANS.

The wasal fortnightly meeting of the abave Board, was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, oa Tuesday. There were present :—Messrs. J. Moseley-Williams Cchairman), Samuel Taylor, A. R. Norman, .1. Meadowcroft, the Rural District Councillors, with G. F. Ashton, (clerk.)

CENTRAL POOR LAW CONFERENCE. Mr. W. Chause, hon. secretary, to the Central Poor Law Conference, forwarded a statement adopted by the committee at their meeting on the 25th February last, which was to be submitted to the annual conference to be held in London early next year. The statement dealt with new rules for the regulation of the proceedings at central conferences, and the Runcorm Guardians were asked to forward any amendments or additions to the statement before the 17th inst. The Board eff-red no amendments or additions. A NEW TRIBUNAL OF APPEAL. ANIMATED DISCUSSION. Mr. John Meadowcroft had given notice that he would move the following resolution:—"With a view to making more oomplete and comprehensive the resolution of the Guardians passed at their meeting on Tufa-idly the sth inst. relating to assessments, it is desirable that all as- sessments or valuations of property be retorted by the overseers to the independent authority named in the previous resolution, and not to Board of Guardians or their Assessment Committees, and that preliminary in- quiries into these matters be held locally, and that ap- pellants be celle I to state their objections wherever an increase is made." Mr. Meadowcroft ebserved it would perhaps be better if the Clerk read the resolution passed on the sth December which he observed had been passed without notice given to the members of the Board. The Clerk then read the minutes referring to the re- cent letter received train the Prescot Board of Guardians petitioning the Runcorn Beard of Guardians to support an application of their's to the Local Gevernment Board for'the establishment of a new court of rating appeal. Mr. Mc,alowcroft, continuing, considered it advan- tageous to have the minutes read, as those who were not present were introduced to the facts of the case. Had he the possession of the elequence and persuasive powers of the Admiral ; he felt lee would not have much difficulty in getting the Board to take up his views. He simply sought to extend the already expressed views of the guardians 'vide newspaper reports. For already they felt that three sectione of assessment, viz., railways, canals, and other public works—and other public works implied, of course, a very large area—should be referred to a special tribunal. Having quoted. from the news- flamer report of Dece.eher 15th's Council meeting, Mr. Meadowcroft pointed out that be agreed with the guardians, and was prepared to tee) that far with them. Those matters were too large and too important for an Assessment Committee or Qaarter Sessions to deal with. and therefore they should be referred to a more impartial tribunal. That he agreed with. But why con- fine themselves to those three branches only? Why should not the whole go to the special tribunal ? He con- tended that petiole were brought for miles around to attend that Assessment Committee to resist an increase of assessment of perhaps two or three pounds. They had to lose a day, and pay railway expanses ; and, even if they proved the:r case,they got no exoenses.Theugh if they went to Quarter Sessions,and got their ease proved they also got their expenses. He urged that all valua- tions and assessments should be dealt with entirely apart from the Board of Guardians. Having criticised the attitude of the several Guerdi ens who had spoken at the meeting referred to Mr. Meadovrcroft formally moved his resolution. Mr. Linaker said he was not prepared to second Mr. Meadavecroft. Be was in the haht of reading the news- paper reports and he woutd defend all the remarks he had made respecting the objection he bad to the Quarter Sessions as a Court of appeal for assessments. He did not however, make any distinction of railways, canals or oth-r public works or anything at all. kle argued that Mr. Meadowcroft had not shown them how he would deal with the matter. The whole of his resolution was wide, and he did not tell them anything definite. As for the Assessment Committee of that B)erl Mr. Linaker thought they did their work very well. It was simply the Quarter Sessions as a court of appeal that he objected to. Mr. Mclntyre, proceeding to argue the case, wished he possessed one quarter of the eloquence of Mr. Meadowcroft to say nothing of the Admiral. (Laugh ter). Mr. Meadowcroft ebjected to the matter being argued by Mr. Mclntyre traces he would be allowed to reply. According to Standing Orders Mr. Mclntyre should con- fine himself to a personal explanation if he liked. Admiral .Jones-Perry: If I second the matter will it be in order? (Laughter.) I don't understand it— (renewed laughter)—acd if I did it would not matter. I will second it. (Increased laughter). Mr. Mclntyre in defence of the attitude taken by the Parliamentary Committee in arriving at the original proposition, argued that the three sections, railways, canals, and other public works were not matters of local importance—they were national affairs. (Hoar, hear.) They could deal with local if sirs themselves, but respecting the others that Board did not possess any confidence in the Quarter Sessions. They might go further, and take a personal view. Mr. Meadowcroft had not proved the incompetency of the Assessment Committee of that Union. He thought Mr. Meadow- croft had said—he was sure be would not deny it—that the Assessment Committee was open to influences. He (Mr. Mclntyre) thought it was a serious charge—(hear. hear)—to bring against that Committee. He also sad he would set up a more efficient and cheaper machinery. He thought it was not worth while going into the ques- tion. (Hear, hear.) Mr. S. Woodward expressed himself as one of the persons named by Mr. Meadowcroft. He was there to say he adhered to all the remarks he had given utter- ance to, and tie wished also to say in reference to the efficiency of the assessment committee.Mr Pleadoweroft seemed to think that some of them had laid most serious charges against the Court of Quarter Sessions. lie thought Mr. Meadowcroft had laid more serious charges against the aesessment committee. When he justified thee charges it would be time enough to reply. Mr. J Meadowcroft in replying said with regard to the remarks of Mr. Linaker respecting the definition of the proposed tribunal. The fact that there was re) definition in the previous resolution was sufficient reply to that. If a court was competent ts deal with the larger questions, which the Guardians were agreed should go before a special tribunal ; surely it was competent to deal with the smaller ones. Mr. Mclntyre: It is a question of expense. Mr. Meadowcroft: There has been no reference to expenses. That is an after thought. Continuing Mr. Meadowcroft observed that he knew the advantage of discussing committee work full well, and in discussing that question he thought it right to bring home to the Board the evil of dealing with those questions piece • meal. They had come to a resolution, he simply sug- gested they should extend it. Speaking of his accus- ation against the assessment committee he said he did not care to prove the committee's incompetency—though doubtless he could do so. He 'anew there were repre- sentatives of large private works upon it, but the rail- way, and canals were not represented, and they never would be: That matter had been brought forward; he was challenged to it or he would not have mentioned it. Finally he accused the Board of keeping in their own hands such matters as they thought right. With regard to all the reflections upon the Quarter Sessions, there were others who would be interested in that and probably defend themselves. . Mr. Woodward proposed that the question be now
put. As the result of the votr. Mr Meadowcroft was opposed by the whole Bo trd including his seconder. Mr. Meadowcroft : I quite expected it. (Genera laughter).

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JANUARY 5, 1900 THE BANKRUPTCY OF MR. WALTER COLLIER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JANUARY 5, 1900 THE BANKRUPTCY OF MR. WALTER COLLIER.
An Unsuccessful Ap-plication.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday be- fore His Honour Judge James an application was made on behalf of Mary Collier, widow a the late Mr. Walter Collier of Runcorn, that the trustee in bankruptcy in the matter of her son,Walter Collier, bankrupt, rejecting her proof of .£5OO be overruled. —Mr, Rhodes of Manchester (instructed by Mr. Eaton) iepresented the applicant and Mr. Cuthbert Smith of Liverpool (instructed by Mr. Unsworth) appeared on behalf of the trustee. Mr. Rhodes in stating the case for the applicant ob- served that the proof of Mary Collier, mother of the bankrupt, was sent in on the 12th September for £5OO. The trustee, notwithstanding the terms on which the debt was alleged to be owing, rejeeted the proof on the 12. h December and the present application was now made for the trustee's action to be overruled. The bankrupt was a grocer and carried on business in several places in Runcorn, Widnes and other centres. He succeeded his father Sarnu4 Collier who died on the Bth October. 1883, and whose will was proved on the 25th October. The late Mr. Collier left his wife, Mary Collier, the sum of £.500 and the residue of the estate was to be equally divided amongst the children. He further provided that the business should be carried on by his executors until his son Walter was of age, and who should then have the opportunity of taking over the business. The establishment was considered to be worth £ll5O and it was decided in 1888 that Walter Col- lier should take over the basiness on paving £l5O to each of the other three children and taking over the debt of £5OO, the legacy to his mother, and paying in- terest upon it. By 1892 he had paid off the three legacies of £l5O each and on the 12th February a COM. veyance was made out in which the property was made. over to Walter Collier. In the cenve7ance it was recited that the £5OO legacy to Mary Collier had been satisfied, but this was done solely in order that he might have a clear title to the property. The £5OO was as a matter of fact still owing, but Mrs. Collier agreed that her son should take it over as a personal liability and that he should continue to pay interest for it. His Honour: Was the interest paid? Mr. Rho : Yes Mr. Walter eller reeularly paid the interest on .2500: The interest was paid as a personal debt to which he was liable to his mother. There was no promissory note given to Mrs. Collier. Tne learned Counsel then eroceeded to read the affidavits of Mrs. Collier, Mi. Walter Collier, and Mr. F. A. Lake. Mr. Cuthbert Smith asked that Mrs Collier might give evidence. Mrs. Collier said she was the widow of Samuel Collier, of Runcorn. and she made the affidavit which appeared in her name. In May, 1888, it was agreed between all parties concerned, that her son, Walter Collier, should take over the business and the property of her late hus- band. Her sand:tad to pay £450 to his brothers and sisters and pay her a leeacy of £5OO for the business. She had never received the money but her son had paid her interest at the rate of 103. a week since that time. She got the money regularly, and she had no other money In live upon. She expected that he would repay her the £5OO which was money left in the business by her late husband, when he could afford. No written agreement was made at the time that her son Waiter should pay her the money. She admitted attaching her signaturelto the:eriginel conveyance new produced which stated that she had received £5OO for the business. She had left the matter in tee hands of her S3licitor and dtd not remember whether the will was read over to her or not. She had made a will but could not tell what was in it, and could not say whether it dealt with the £5OO. In reply to Mr. Modes she said the £5OO was all that she had and therefore the will must deal with that

amount. Walter Collier. the bankrupt, was then called and said there was an agreement with regard to the bu, aess as produced ire court. Na other agreement was made but it was understood that he was to repay his mother.'s £5OO for the business and in the meantime he had to pay her 5 per cent interest on that amount. This money was paid regularly every week but it did not appear in his cash book as interest but was included in items as paid to "self." The money he pail to his mother was at the rata of 104 per week. Apart from the profits made in the business he had no other means of paying the money but at the time the £5OO was put in the business it was perfectly solvent. His Honour said that in the face of the agreemeat which had been produced in court with Mrs Collier's signature, he could do no other than refuse the applica- tion. He had no doubt that Mrs Collier was anxious to help her son in life and that she put her money in the business in order to help him to carry it on. The amount which her son had paid to her seemed to him to be a contribution to her and not in the nature of inter- est. Mrs. Collier lived in one of the branch shops of her son and at appeared to him that the payments her son made to her were for the purpose of supporting her. There was no doubt that the business at first was a good ,business and that her son expected to be able to maintain his property but in his(lais Honour's) opinion the money was not putin the form ot a loan but in the form of keeping the business going and as part of the business. He felt very sorry for Mrs. 'Collier but he could not give any other decision than refuse the application. Mr. Cuthbert Smith suggested that the costs be taken out of the estate. His Honour acceded to his request.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[BY A CORRESPONDENT.] The Runcorn Anglers' Association are arranging for a zonsignment of full grown trout with which to stock their waters, and when this is done the prospects of capital sport will be brighter than ever.

Mr J. Meadowcroft, at the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, took an isolated stand upon the question of a special tribunal for the hearing of rating appeals? Though so greatly outnumbered at the vote, it does not follow that Mr Meadowcroft had no argument upon his side—for he bad; and good sound argument has long been advanced as to the inefficacy of the present system of as-88s- meat. Further Mr. Mtadowcroft simply desired to go the whole way in supporting the Prescot Board of Guardians, who have come by their resolution ; no doubt, after due deliberation and not from sheer opposition to individuals. It was evident that several of the Runcorn Guardians looked upon Mr. Meadowcroft as an obstructionist, and whether he was backed up by reason or argument, seemed to have no consideration with them, and in the end he got out-voted, or in his own words "just what he expected."

Mr.Nleadowcroft pointed out very clearly that the Parliamentary Committee were themselves agreed that the Court of Quarter Sas3ions was not impartial enough to deal with "railways, canals, and other public works," and they were prepared to go that far with the Prescot Union. Those being the principal objeeions in assesiment work, it was only natural that someone should ask, why the " satellites' should not go with their sun ? But because Mr. MeP.dowcroft asked the question, and because in doing so he told some hard truths about, Assessmens Committees in general, the sinceptibili- ties of the Guardians were touched, and therein roused. Sentiment prevailed and all argument flew Ito the winds. The little incident, however, illus- trates that he who would secure a following on the Runcorn Board of Guardians must fell his ground carefully.

The Local Goverumenti Board have torwarded sanction for the borrowing of .E 4,000 and intimate that the money, principal and interest, should be repaid in 23 years. This has alarmed even the.pro- moters of the scheme to such an extent that Mr.W, Handley advised applying to the Local Govern- ment Board for an" extension of time." It will be remembered that calculated as repayable for a period of 30 years, the expense worked out to some- thing like lid. in the £ increased rate,which would have to be faced. Reducing the time to 23 years naturally increases the rate to slightly over 21.,but 'it also has this advantage -it will be the sooner cleared off. As I have said repeatedly the Council have nothing to be ashamed of in showing" a park and pleasure ground for ..Zl.OOO. Indeed compared with " a waterworks "at £70,000 odd, it is a stroke of economical business. Whether the time limit is extended or not matters little if the scheme goes on.

NEW YEAR FESTIVITIES AND PROSPECTS.
A Brighter Outlook.

The pessine of the old yoar took place somewhere between Sunday and Monday last. There was nothi.,g that especially marked the change, but the usual customs prevailing at the heralding in of year after year. Watch-night services were held in the several places of worship and were largely attended. The peals at the Parish Church tolled for the passing of the old and rang sweetly on the advent of the New Year. Up to twelve o'clock the large numbers of people who par- aded the streets coneueted themselves with becoming decorum, but Ile sooner had the old year and the Sun- day passed away than the scene became considerably more animated. And far into the small hours of the morning the" ragtag and bobtail" could be heard in- dulging in noisy mirthfulness, whilst others were strugeling with the problem of sleep. The year 1899, has been to the tradesman and artisan of Runcorn an improvement upon its predecessor 1898. True, the improvement has not been very marked, but it has been consisLent and steady. There have heel a few failures, and one or two small strikes, or rather dis- agreements between capital and labour; yet talvn, alto- gether, they have been so insignificant that the twelve month just concluded can well be termed a fairly suc- cessful oue. Again the number of empty houses in the town, though still large, has greatly diminished from what it was in 1898, and there a,re prospects that a still further decrease will occur in 1900. Another item of importance which the last year saw recorded was the return of Runcorn to its former position in the football world. And duriug the 1899 portion of this present season, the performance of the club has been really praiseworthy. We wish them success in 1900 ; bat from the conduct of one or two of the players, it seems likely that the club may again sink to the low level of 1898, or worse. Still let us hope and wish for the beat. In regard to our staple indus- tries, there appears to be no change likely to occur that will deprive us of them. They are staple still—with the exception,of course,of one—and the increases whsch are being made le others at Weston, Weston Point, Old Quay, and Widnes will more than fully compensate for any loss. All this is a matter for congratulation. Writing last year we observed "Runcorn would not become an ideal town until the District Council " taxed" the inhabitants more in- the nature of "saving them from themselves." And we spoke of the stvets of deteriorated and dilapidated property which remained eyesores, and fever hot bads here and there throughout our town. Deducting those few houses which have since become inhabited, there has been little or nothing done by the Wstrict Council to compel the owners to mend their ways. The only step taken has been the prosecution of a few urchins (by certain property owner) for alleged damage to their already uninviting property. So we repeat the town will neeer be an ideal one whilst its sanitary affairs are treated With indiffereece. Notwithstanding this indiffer- ence in the past, the Council may retrieve the lest pres- tige of the town—for what but the lost prestige of the town makes the ordinary folk leave it to do their shop- ping elsewhere, notably Liverpool—by attending to tem matters with a view to keeping the native at home. There is talk, too, of a bridge across the Mersey ; Elec- tric Light for the town ; a tramway through it; a park and pleasure ground ; an additional telephone service, and other good things. If half these schemes materialise, there is hope for us yet.

div.head: MERSEY MiSSION TO SEA MEN
div.p: MERSEY MiSSION TO SEA MEN
RUNCORN BRANCH.
Annual Tea Party and Concert.

The annual tea party and concert held on Wedne ; lay evening in connection with the above Mission was Imre largely attended by masters of vessels, sailors and boat- men and the proceedings were characterized by great enthusiasm. A sumptuous tea was nrovided, the management being in the bands ef the following lades: —Mesdames Abel, Stokes, Digges. Summerfield, Harri- son; Walker, McLennan, Grounde, Price, Dyer, Johnson, A. Abel, Dykes, Ambeman, and Miss W. Heasley. The seafaring community and boat people thoroughly enjoyed the feast of good things to which they had been invited (free of charge) and they appre- ciated none the less the efforts to entertain them at the concert which followed. The room, which was packed to its utmost capacity, had been tastefully decerated with flags and bunting, and displayed in con- spicuous letters were such greetings as " Welcome to our Sailors,"." Welcome to the visitors." Mr. J K Digges presided, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. E. Lambert, M.A. (chaplain). Rev W Scholes, Messrs. J Stokes, and W Shaw (Missionary). The Chairman opened the proceedings by wishing all present a happy and prosperous New Year. They had had a very successful year, and the weekly concerts had been quite as crowded as the room was 1 that evening- • Indeed the attendances had been so large that he thought they bad made a mistake in net securing more ground, and having a larger building. During the summer months, through the kindness of a number of ladies, sailors had enjoyed picnics to Halton and Frodsham, and he wished it to be known that all the sailors were equally welcome, on these occasions. They were always glad to see them at the institute, and he could assure them that Mr Shaw (missionary) was just in his element when he amid shake bands with a sailor and bring him to that place. (Applause.) Daring an interval in the programme The Rev. E. Lambert proposed a hearty vote of thanks to all those who had assisted to make the proceedings a success, including the ladies who had dispensed the tea, the friends who had pr•mided the entortainment,and the ladies and gentlemen who had tubscribed to the funds. He was glad to come there to see improvements. For instance he found himself standing on a much larger platform than he had stood upon before,and he felt his position very much firmer than previously. It was always a good sin when they came to broaden their platform and felt it firmer under them. He was glad to hear they were getting a few large ships at Runcorn like the Puritan and others. They welcomed the strangers from these ships, away from their homrs, and they hoped all thee men who belonged to the big ships and the coasters would come to that institute, and make the place their home as much as possible. By do- ing that they would enable the Mersey Mission to fulfil Re very first duty. The perform- ance of the children that evening would 1 doebtless remind them of their own homes. A little child could often lead them to better things, and it was one of the greatest compliments that had ever been paid tn seamen that as a class they were child-like not simple- ton!,tfhoer g i ve Masteranaa usedre receptivity term—thativity which and ds theireh exhibited by friends Caht rti an te. apnadriha ihs Apostleschnreh . ay n ap p pre-eminently. flh 1 teey whisalbsdeudat larnlelattdhhieen7w"jaoytr:ers connected with that Institute and

prosperous 15:!yr Year. (Applause.) Mr. Shaw seconded the vote of thanks. Referring to the work of the Mission he said he liked to try and blip not only seamen,but_ilatrnen. and blat people generAlly.

They were all invited to make full use of the institute and to attend all the services and meetings in con- nection with it. It delighted him to see so large an audience present, and he hoped they had all thoroughly enjoyed what had been readily provided for them on that occasion. (Applause.) The services of Mr Digges in the chair were suitably acknowledeed on the motion of Mr Stokes seconiled by the Rev W Scholee. Mrs Absl then distributed to the seamen, bottmen,and host-lads. number of woollen mufflers whicle are an annual aift from the mission workers. The programme opened with a pianoforte solo by Miss Garvie which proved a good intro luetion to t proceedings. Miss Coward gave a cre lit able rendering of" Our Jack's come home to-day," and was loudl7 ap- plauded. The next item, a humorous piece by Mr T Woods, fairly captivated the audience, and the artiste was reealled. The little Misses L Shaw and A Coward ' followed with that ever popular duet " I don't want to play in your yard" and needless to say the selection ap- pealed irresistibly to the sailors who voted an encore. The little folks responded by repeating the last verse of the piece. Mine Garvie then sane with touch feeling "For old time's sake" which also appeared to find great favour with the Jack tars pre- sent. A sweet pin-. of music on the mandoline by Miss M. Diggee was cordially acknowledged and Master J. Rutter was the subject of an ovation for his spirited rendering of "Scarlet and Blue" Nme the less success- ful WAg the animated performance of " Soldiers of the Queen," by Master F. Outhwaite assisted by Masters W Shaw, and L 'rooks, and Misses L. Shaw. and Amy Coward. " TreCT suspicious "by Mise Ceward and Mr. C. Temple was a most diverting, duet, and the roam fairly shook with laughter and applause. The second part of the programme was equal in every respect to the first. It consisted of humorous soetes by Mr. .T. Wood : " Shoulder to shoulder "by Master L Tonke ; " Delly's Revenge "by Mica Coward ; "The cows are in the Clover " by Miss Hill; " Ship Britta,nia, " Mister J Rutter ; and " As your hair grows whiter," by Miss Garvie. Mr. Woods and Master Rutter received well deserved encores. The acc.emnani=t for the evening was Miss Garvie. At the I close of the proceedings the company sang the National Anthem.

WELCOMING THE NEW COUNT COURT JUDGE. Congratulatory Speeches at Warrington. His Honour Gwynne James held his first court at Warrington on Thursday morning. There was a large attendance of solicitors, including Messrs. Longton, Browne, Jenkins, Forahaw, Dobson, Long. land, Unsworth, Fowler, Steele, Wallhead, Roberts, Draper, and E. A. White. When his Honour took his seat at ten o'clock Mr. LOW iTON said that before the commencement of the business he should like to be permitted, on behalf of the local solicitors who practised in the come, to say a few words. Tney congratulated his Honour very heartily and sincerely upon his appointment to such a high position. They considered it was a high position. The EngUsh judicial Bench had always been of a higb standard with regard to ability, and the character of the eccupants had also been of a high standard. They quite felt from what they knew of his Honour that in his hands those traditions would he maintained. On behalf of the solicitors practising in tbat Court he could say that they would at all times do their utmost te support the dignity of the judge's position. Whatever knowledge of law they could bring not only in the inter- cats of their own clients, as they were in duty bound to do, but else in some measure—they hoped in a consider- able measure—to assist his Honour to arrive at the truth of the case, and towards the better administration nf jastice. They hoped his Honour would be blessed with good health, aaa live long to fulfil his duties to the satisfaction of the suitors who came before him, (Hear, hear.) Mr. Beowsin said he had been told that it would 13, hardly fittine if he were ant to join lathe compliments, as one of the leaders at the court, and extend to the Judge his hearty coegratulations on his succession to the offiee. They had been accustomed to a good old judge for a reat number of years, and it was with sorrow that he heard he was leaving them, but it was with equal gladness they welcomed his successor, know- ing that he had come off a good old legal stock. There were several items in the practice of the court that had been allowed in the circuit since the year 184.7, and one was that the defendant's solicitor had no right to rep!y. He thought that was a good rule. He did not know whether his Honour proposed to extend the practice or not. They had only to wait and see, but it was a prac- tice which. had been long adopted, His Horrous : Da you think that it is a goad prao tics? Mr. littowsz in reply said that ie Rayed a great deal of unnecessary talk, and he thought it was a good practice and one which be ventured to think, his Honour could follow safely. Ile had only to say, in conclusion, that the solicitors practising in that court treseed his Honour would be spared for many years to preside over the court. (Hear, hear.) His Honour replying to the cordial welcome and con- gratulation% said he thanked them most sincerely for the kind welcome they had accorded to him. He came before them as a comparative s..ranger, and therefore it was all the more gratifying to him to roceive Such a welcome, on this the first oceashan of hie sitting in a Lancashire court, and also to be assured ot the cordial co-operation of those who practised before hie. He knew that he suceeeded a gentleman who had presided in that court, and over ttee other courts ia the circuit, for a very (great nuciber of years, and who during that lengthened period had administered justice to the entire satisfaction of the clients %led of the public, and who, if he might say se, to use le words of Mr Lengton, had maintained the traditib a of theoffice he held. He could only hope that he ,deht prove himself a not unworthy successor. With regard to the point raised by Mr. Breeme. he might say that he entirely agreed with the rule When prectising at the bar on a few occasiens hohe.4 disagreed with that rule. and he must say that on t tose occasions he had appeared on behalf of defendants who had a very bed case. (Laugh- ter.) However, the rule was a just one, which he should continue to adopt. He should endeavour as far as pos- sible in presiding over that court so to act that all the business which was put down for a particular day should if poslible, be finished on that day, and in this respect he was sure that he should have the cordial co- operation of those who practised before him. There should be no remnants, as in his view the County Court was a poor man's court, and the fact of a day's delay—a man haying to coma there on two occasions— must mean the loss of a day's labour or a day's wages. Therefore, he trusted that as far as poseible they would finish off all the work that was put down for each nerticular day. He thanked thern most sincerely for the kind welclme they had eiven him on this his first visit to this court and to Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Later on congratulations were tendered by Ur Cuthbert Smith, barrister, Liverpool, and Mr. Rhodes, barrister, Mancheeter. His HONOUR, in reply, said it was always a great pleastsre to him to see members of his own profession because ho knew he would always receive their assist- ance as he was sure he should receive the assistance of the other branches of the profession.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

YOUNG WARRINGTON THIEVES —A LIKING FOft STOUT. At the Warrington Police Court on Saturday, five boys named James Brookes, &IMPS Tranter. Thomas Brace- girdle, Alfred Stephens and Ernest Stephens, were charged with stealing from a cart in Wiuwick-road, at 5.30, the previcus afternoon, seven bottles of porter, the property of Greenall,Whitley and Co.—They all pleaded guilty with the exeeption of Brockese—The Chief Con- stable stated the facts of the ease. He said that at 530 on Friday afternoon one of the drays belonging to Messrs Greenall Whitley and Co., in charge of a man named Henry Hamer was in the neighbourhood of the " florss and Jockey " Inn, delivering bottles of stout. It was dark at the time. The driver left the dray in which were a number of Cases con- taining bottles of stout with no one in charge a hilst he delivered some stout. He noticeelte;tbe boys" hang- ing "about the eehicle when he left it and when he came back he saw th,m running away. He followed them and caught Braceeirdle and found a bottle of stout in his possession. Be exananiecl his stock and found there were seven or eight bottles missing. Bracegirdle immediately gave the names of the other prisoners and that of a toy who was too young to be brought before the Ccurt. Information was given to the police and the boys were arrested by Sergeant Eirans. Although Brookes pleaded not gui(ty he replied .in answer to the charge "I took one." Trat,tr raid ha took two, Braceeirdle one, Alfred Stephens two' and Ernest Stephens one.—The Chairman (to Brookes) : Did you not take one ?.—Brookes: I had it" gave "to rue. —Evidence in support of the Chief Constable's statement was given by Henry Hamer, the driver of the dray,and P.S Evans, who arrested the boy.—None of the pri- soners had anything to say.—The Chief Constable said Brcokes and Brategirdle had previously been before the court and were fined 5.3. fhe Chairman (to prisoners) : We shall make you remember this eecapade of yours. You will each receive six strokes with the birch rod and be kept in the cells till six o'clock and I think you will remember it.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

FRIDAY. —Before—the Mayor (In the chair), Alderman Wright. Councillor Smethurst. and Mr 3. Hepherd. PILFERING AN AUTOMATIC MACHINE. - Joseph Frederick Plumb. Slutcher's-lane, and Arthur Langstaff, 325. Knots- ford-road, fifteen years of ag., were charged with stealing 43 boxes of chocolate value 3s 7d, from an automatic machine at Arpley Station, the property oc the Sweetmeat Automatic Con4any, Limited.—Detectiee Howells of the London and North-Western Railway Company said that on the first of December he received information of a robbery having taken place from an automatic machine at Arpley Station. He ex- amined the machine and found one glass broken and found that the machine had been damaged with some blunt instru- ment. He made inquiries and in consequence of what he was told he saw the defendant Langstaff and told him of what had occurred; but he dewed having committed the rob • bery. He then went to Plumb and told him that he and Lang- staff were suspected of the theft. Plumb at first said he knew nothing about it but afterwards said that at two o'clock in the morning on December Ist he saw Langstaff in the goods yard, and asked him if he would go to Latchford with him to call some men up. Langstaff said he would and asked him if be was going through Arpley Staticn. Plumb replied that he was. Langstaff said "Are you going to break into that slot 9" and he replied "No we wid get into a bother." When they got to the station Langstaff went up to the machine, took out an old hammer,smashed the glass and told Plumb to take some chocolate out. Plumb said ha took out eleven boxes and handed them to Langstaff and he gave him four boxes back. They then went on to Latch o. d and came back the same way but Plumb said they did not touch the machine again. He (Detective Howells) told him that 43 boxes were missing and he said "We left some in " Both the youths were servants of the company. but since the robbery they had been discharged. The machine had been broken into several times Leyore.—Bach of the defendants dented taking 43 boxes. They said they only took eleven.—Defendants were severely reprimanded and fined 10s. and co6ts each (£1 Os. 6d.) in all. NEGLECT OF OHILDREN. —ALL THROUGH DRINIC.-38113e$ Rawlinson' 2. Mill-yard, Fennel-street, was summonei for neglecting his four children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injary to health on December 15th and other dates.—He pleaded guiltv.—Mr. Browne appeared on behalf of the N*P.O C. He said the case arose on account on the man's drunken habits. He was a labourer at the wireworks and could earn 2Es a week. There was a son earning 6s, making a total weekly income of 341. On the 15th lust, Inspector, Hackett visited the house and found defendant's wife and four children In the front room shivering with cold. It was an ertremely cold day. /and snow was on the ground, but there was no fire in the grate and no Mod in the house. The children were fairly well clothed but poorly nourished. The house was fairly well furnished and clean, so that the wife was not to blame. Defendant would not give her any m-ney to bny food with. It was a bad case.—Defendant was sent to gaol for fourteen days —George Morrell, 2. Daikin's-yard. was committed to gaol for 14 days for a similar offence. This case was also the result of drink. SATIINDAY.—Before Messrs. T. Birchall (in the chair) and It _ T. Fairclough,

Two MONTHS FOR ASSAULT ON THE. POLVF..—Jameg Quig- ley was charged on a warrant with assaulting P.C. Taylor OD the 23rd December.—P.C. Taylor said that on the night of the date in question he was called to a public-house in Winwick-road for the purpose of arresting a man named Moran who was brought before the magistrates and sent to prison for a month. Whilst he was arresting the man he was assaulted by Quigley. and set upon by a number of members of the crowd which surrounded him. He had his helmet knocked off, and the chin strap was broken He was very roughly handled. Two young men named Stirrup and Brad- bury eame to his assistance and they were assaulted. Prisoner got hold of witness's arm and tried to pull him away from Moran. When he and Morals w.-re struggling on the ground Quigley struck him in the face and on the back of the neck. —The Chief Constable said Quigley had been before the Court, 13 times for assaulting the police, drunkenness, and for inflicting grievous bodily harm on his parents, for which he had six months. He was one of the worst characters in the town. If it was not for such men as Bradbury and Stirrup the life of the policeman would be worth nothing in that neighbourhood.—Prisoner was committed to goal for two months with hard labour.
TUESDAY.—Before Mr. T Birthsll (In the chair), and Mr.
W. Owen.

THE THEFT FROM A WAITING Roox.—ln the Case Of Elizabeth Ockleshaw, Clifton-street, Higher Crumpsall, who was remanded the previous Tuesday on a charge of stealing several articles from a waiting room at the Central Station. the Chief Constable said that Mr. White, the Magistrates' Clerk, had handed him a document which he tmd received from the Medical Officer at Strangeways gaol. King-street, was summoned for being drunk in charge of a horse and cab in tiuttermarket-street on the 25th December.—P.o Metcalf said that at 12.15 on Christmas Day he saw the defendant driving a horse and cab up Buttermarket-street. lie was very drunk and was swaying to and fro en the box. —The Chief Constable said the defendant had been before the Court three times in the. year 1899. for being drunk in charge, At Christmas timp the public safety was endangered by such men.—A fine of 106 and costs was imposed. OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—WiIiiSM Hewitt, 11, Dutton-street, was fined 5s and costs for making use of obscene language in Dutton-street on December 17th.

FuRIOUS DRIVING —"THIRTEEN MILES AN HOUR IN HvIDOE-STREET."—Obristian &Avers, butcher of Appleton Cross. was summoned for furiously driving a horse and trap in R. idge-street on December 22nd. —He pleaded not guilty. Smith stated thit at 7-25 on the morning of the 22nd De amber he was on duty in Bridge-street, when he saw the defendant driving a horse and trap from the direction of Warrington Bridge. The horse was going at a "flying speed" of abr ut thirteen miles an hour. There was another vehiele going in the same direction at a good speed and the defendant passed it. He drove up Bridge-street till the ttap came into contact with a lorry and he then had to pull up. He saw the defendant at nine o'clock and told him he would be reported. He said he did not consider he was driving furiously.—James Briers, a carter in the en,ploy of Mr. Isherwood, contractor, and P.C. Dawson, having given evid- ence, defendant, who had been before the Court twice before for similar offences. was fined 20s including costs. FIRING A GUN NEAR THE HIGHWAY.—EIIiott Harris, 42, Cumberland-street, was summoned for firing a gun within fifty yards of the highway on the 17th December.—P.S. Smith said that at 11 o'clock on the date in question, he was proceeding along the Bridgewater Canal Bank from Black- bear Bridge to Wilderspool, when he saw defendant with a guu, standing near the new road leading from Wilderspool- road to Wash-lane. He fired at a sea-gull. Witness took his name and address and reported him.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed. div.head: LOAN
div.p: THE LOAN

The CLERK said he hao received a letter from the Public Works Loan 13oard, to the effect that the loan money (27,000) would be receivable as from December 20cii, from which elite interest would run. He had received the following circular letter from the Local Government B3ard dated 14th December, with copy of notice issued by the Treasury :—" They oirect by their minute of 2nd November, that on loans granted subse- quent to that date the rat( $ of interest will vary from 3 to 314 cer cent." The Clerk stated that it was satisfac- tory to note that the efforts made in the Board's behalf, had resulted in the consent to a loan of £7,003 at £2 154 per cent. THE FURNISHING CF THE INFIRMARY.

Toe Infirmary Committee submitted the following re- commendations :—That the Board be recommended to approve the scheme submitted by the furnishing sub- committee, arid to sanction the purnhase of articits and the execution of the work in accordance therewith, and that the furnishing sub-committee be empowered to do all that they may den necessary for carrying out the scheme in the most efficient and economical manner, submit ing recommendations in respect of orders either for the supply of goods or the employment of labour to be passed at any ordinary meeting of the Board, but that no enlargement of the scheme snail- be mad i except after written notice, and at a special meeting of the Guardians. Mr. WILLIAM Houuryrori proposed the adoption of the minutes of the Infirmary Committee and said the sub- committee had evidently gone into their work thoroughly. The schedule and report were adopted unanimously.

div.head: CHRISTMAS DAY AFFAIR.
div.p: THE CHRISTMAS DAY AFFAIR.

From the miWte; ofilTiTiTfouse Committee it appeared that the committee regretted to say that five women in- mates of the house got over the garden wall ia the after part of Christmas Day, taking clothing with them be- longing to the institution. They were arrested, and when charged by the police sad—" Yes, we did. We had a drop of beer in the house in the morning and that set ul off." Toe result of the trial was that all were imrri3onrd. The minutes were confirmed, on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. HICKMAN.

-- -- The Board then went into committee for the purpose of making the appointment of a medical officer for the Haydock district and one for the Newton district. The candidates for the Haydock district were Dr Thomas , Ernest Hayward (48), of Haydock; and Dr Arthur DJwl- ing (32), also of Haydoek. The testimonials were read and the candidates called into the room ,eparately and qucstioned by the Chairman and other members of the Board. Dr Dowling was eventually unanimously ap- pointed. The Board then proceeded to the appointment of an officer for the Newton district. The candidates were—Dr Harold E Watkins (31), Stone Legh, Newton ; Dr William Valentine (38), Market-square, Earlestown ; Dr Percy R Ga.age (28), Wargrave-road, Earlestown ; Dr Charles J Mouncey (40), Earlestown ; and Dr W Latham (34), Cross-lane, E alestown. Dr. Patterson (50), Lismore House, Earlestown, was originally, one of the candidates, but he withdrew befa.re the meeting of the Board. The voting resulted in the appointment of Dr Valentine.:The two doctors were also appointed pub- lic vaccinators. The Board then rose.

The Re‘. E. R. Tarbuck on the War.

The Vicar of St. Paul's Church (the Rev: E R. Tar- buck), preaching on Sunday evening gave an exhaustive summary of the work which had been accomplished in the parish during the past year. Alluding to the war, he said For some time we have been engaged, after many and many a long year of comparative peace, in a war against a foe whose subjugation demands all our energies, and whose courage is equal to our own. We have awakened to the fact that we have only just escaped being the victims of a fah-reaching conspiracy to over- throw our supremacy in South Africa ; and whilst we are learning important lesions at a great cost we are- proving that the bravery of our soldiers and sailors is quite up to that of former times. We are greatly encouraged by the loyalty of the colonies of the empire, as'd we are glad to see that the lie has been given to that old sneer that our Yeomanry and Volunteers were merely eitivn soldiers playing at war. The enthusiasm that has teen awakened by our reveries has probable called forth an answer Oa the appeal that has been made by the War Office for volunteers that has opened the eyes of the world at large. It has been a surprise to those on the Continent who have for many years sneered at these portions of our reserve strength. May God bring the war to an end soon, and with as little mischief as pos- sible.
