div.head: NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE. SENIOR COMPETITION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE. SENIOR COMPETITION.
Warrington v. Swinton.

Warrington met Swinton on the ground of the latter on Saturday last, when considerable interest was take in the encounur. The matches between the two clubs are almost always close affairs, and the fact that Sw ton have never yet won at Warrington makes the en- counter all the mire speculative and exciting. Warring- ton were not quite at full strength on Saturday, as Fish was unable to play in addition to Bate being al absentee. Hockenhad filled the vacancy, while the home side turned out as selected. Though the weathe was fine the state of the ground milltsted against War- rington's chances, for they are entirely unaccustomed to running in three inches Ot oat hthks. A crowd of about 6,000 assembled, and the teams were under the control of Mr. W. M'Cutcheon (Oldham). They were composed as follows :

Swinton: J Goodman, full back, J Lewis, R J Messer, J Taylnr, and V H4mpson threequarters, " Dai" Divies and Morgan, half backs ; Evans. Holmes, Jones, Vigors, Pollitt, Hayes, Preston. and Murpny, forwards. Warrington: J Boscow, full back; E T Jones, L Smith, D Isherwood, and T Elockenh4ll, tlareequarters ; J Duckworth and Allen, half backs; Taylor, Morrison, Boardman, Scholtze, Mereweather, Elea, Hatton and Fairhurst. forwards. .

Warrtngton won he toss and played with the all vi strong breeze at the commencement, Evans setting the ball in motion. The first scrimmage took place at War- rington 25. Duckworth, Allen. and Jones passed, but little ground was gained. Swinton were the next to gain possession, and a chzzling round of pissing by Davies, Morgan, Messer, Taylor, and Lewis, resulted in a try the last named crossing at the corner and sprintiag round the posts. Goodman failed to kick a goal from the easy place. Warrington were not disheartened by this reverse, and a free kick was the moaus of play being transferred to the Swinton territory. Duckworth and Jones got sway and the home line was la great danger for a minute or two. Swinton cleared. but Joaes pun- ted back strongly awl Isherwood upset Lewis. G., od- man met a similar fate when trying to run the toall out. Taylor picked up and nearly got in under the Swinton goal, where play wagccl hotly for some time. Smith was held just inside the rut, but W,rtington kept pegging away. Duckworth secured and throwing wide to Isherwood, the latter drew Taylor and Lewis on to Hockenhall and then dolged over cleverly. Jones kicked a goal. but the whistle had sounded for a free kick, and he failed at the second attempt. The teams were now, on level terms, and went at it warmly. Swinton came away with a rush, Lewis being prevented from seoring by Bosco w, who pushed 'the ilicr in touch at the corner. Warring- ton bad an anxious time, Allen eventually relieving with a fine kick to centre. Here Jonea'Auickly saappsd a Swinton pass and had a clear course wnen the whis:le sounded for a slight knock-on. Some tight scrimmaging followed in the Warrington half, Morgan making a pocr attempt to drop a goal. A mull by Goodman was the means of giving Warrington the advantage, and some smart passing ought to have resulted in a try but Elockenhall made a weak effort to pass Lewis. Then Taylor had a grand chanco' but just t the critical moment he was pulled down from behind. A five yards scrimmage followed, and Isherwood dashed over only to be too late to keep the bill in play. Another spurt was made by Swinton, but to no avail, and half-time arrived with the score a try each:. _ _ _ _

Jones restarted and PoHitt marked. Boacow made a mistake in trying to double, and was tackled near the line. Warrington were hard pressed until a deal ball gave them an opportunity of clearing. Swinton got nicely going with good passing, only to fail through Taylor's poor feeding of Hampson. Play remained at centre until flampsan snapped Duck wortifs pass and sprinted over the Warrington line in fine style, to the joy of the borne crowd. There was no goal, but the Swintonians began to breathe more freely. Davies was penalised, and Jones's kick carried play to the line, War- rington having hard luck in not gettting a try. The home backs went in for defensive tactics, and Warring- ton could make little headway. The game was contested generally in midfield until Davies led another onslaught on the Warrlng,ton goal, wh'cla had some narrow escapes. There was no further scoring, and the play was even to the close. Swinton won by the narrow margin of two tries to one.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES,
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES,
WARRINGTON DEFEAT HULL. A Splendid Game.

The Hull team whicti visited Warrington was not fully representative, but it was a strong combination for all that, including as it did, Taylor,Driscoll and Franks,and Keane, the famous American sprinter. Warrington turned out as selected, but were short of Pate, Fish, and Harris. The weather was favourable and a fair-sized holiday crowd assembled to witness the game though it was not a league match. Hull defeated Warrington earlier in the season by 10 points to 9,and the homesters were naturally eager to avenge themselves. Mr. F. Kennedy, Brocghton, was the referee, and when tie teams lined up in the order given below there would be about 4,000 people present. Warrington: Boscow, full back ; Jones, Smith,Teher- wood, and Hoekenhall, threequarters ; Duckworth and Allen, half-backs ; Taylor, Boardman, Mereweather, Eden, Scholtz:, Fairhurst, Hatton, and Morrison, for- wards.

Hull : Taylor, full back ; Loftbouse, Mahoney, Dris- coll. and Keane, threequartera ; Franks and Trowel!, half-backs ;Wiles, Fildes, Rhodes, Voyce, Harmer, Hun- ter, Sowerby and Holmes forwards. The visitors won the toss and had the advantage of the breeze for the first half. Taylor kicked off for War- rington, the ball going in touch. Hull early took up the attack, Keane tackling Isherwood in the home half Franks and Lofthouse put in some nice play on the opposite wing, but the last named was pushed in touch. Bescow had his kick charged down by Voyce and a score , wasonly averted by the ball going dead. Duckworth andStnith got away cleverly,the latter making a beauti- ful opening for Jones, who knocked on at the critical moment. Exciting play in the visitors quarters followed, Duckwcrtn being held on the line by the diminutive Franks. Warrington heeled out smartly and a quick bout of passing by Deck worth, ' Smith and Jones resulted in a try at the corner. Jones failed to improve his point. Hull got back to centre. but a fine punt by Jones and splendid follow-up by Mereweather resulted in Taylor being grassed near the goal. Warrington attacked with spirit, and the coin- bination being good Jones scored again at the corner from Smith's pass. No goal resulted. The visitors rallied and Driscoll got away but was stopped by Hockenhall when getting dangersus. A flying kick by Hull gave Keane a chance to sprint up, but Isherwocd saved coolly. A premature tackle of Taylor by Eden lost a lot of ground and Hull pressed. Franks got the ball out quickly and threw to Mahoney who was tackled. Smith raised the siege by snapping up the bell and running through the thick of his oppon- ents to the Hull 25 line, where Morrison took the pass and was safely held by Taylor. Boscow did a smart bit of work in following his kick and wetting Keane near the Hull line. Allen made an excellent attempt to score, but was upset, while Hockenhall got as far as the corner flag a moment later. Half-time came with the score 2 tries to nil in favour of Warrington. Wiles restarted and no return being made, Hull as- sumed the aggressive, only to be quickly repelled. Isherwood took the ball and beating Keane gave to Hockenhull, who ran and repassed, Isherwood returning at the prcper moment, and Hockenhall put the finishingltouch on alfirst-class movement in capital style. The try was a really superb ene, and was heartily cheered. Jones tried at goal, but the angle was again too great for him. Warrington maintained the upper hand, the conbination among the backs being unusually fine. Smith and Jones were continually troubling Hull on the right, awl their efforts de- served the cheering they got. Driscoll tackled Jones once when he seemed all over a scorer. Hull now played 5 threequarters, Fildes coming out to check the easing. The trick worked well but Isherwood had hard luck once in failing by inches after a speedy dash. Jones almest landed a penalty goal. Hull at last got into the home half by means of a dribble. Driscoll contributed a tricky run but failed to pass Boscow. and the end soon came with Warrington leading by 3 tries (9 points) to Hull nil.
LANCASHIRE " A " TEAMS COMPETITION.
WARRINGTON " A " v. SWINTON '6 A."
This match was played on the Wilderspool Enclosure on Saturday afternoon before a goad number of spectators. Swinton was well represented, their team including

Pearson. After the rspening exchanges. Bwinton quickly assumed the aggresslyei„ and a try WAS scored from which a goairesulte,.l. Stung by this early reverse, the Warrington team played up pluckily and W Dakin from a scramble near the iice scored. Ho !croft kicked a goal. Wa,rringtort continued to have the best of the play and thete was soms combined work in the open. A _beautiful passing movement ended in Jewkes scoring near the touch line. No goal resulted. The whistle sounded for half-time with Warrington lead- ing by eight points to three. Aided by the wind,Swinten made their way into the Warrington 25 and scored their seuind try from which Pearana 'landed a goal. The teams were now equal„and astern straggle for supremacy wa a made by both sides. Warrington took up the attack and from a scrimmage near the line, Bob Bate picked up and tc3red an unimproved try. Trio weight of the Swint4u men afterwards logan to tell and trom now until the close of tne match the visitors had the most of the game. They .succeeded in scoring two additional tries from which on, goal was kicked. and eventually ran out winners by 16 punts to 11. much to the dis- appointment of the local spec,:ators.

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. [By "Ovalist."] The holiday football has agaiu resulted in a loss of points for Warrin.qton, .but therellas been no loss of prestige, as at Christn3a.. Saturday's match was a stiff one, for Warrington had to beard the lion in his den by going to Swinton, where they were defeated by two tries to one. *On Monday the famous Hull team visited Wilderspool and after a most enjoyable game Warrington's superiority was manifested by a score of three tries to nil. Unfortunately the match was only a" friendly," so that no particular advantage accrued to VKarrington through their success.

Swintonians have a wholesome respect for Warring- ton and they were by no means confident of success on Siturday. Their fears proved to be justified, for with a little luck the result would have been just the opposite to what it was. In fact, so well matched were the teams, [ll4 I believe Warrington would have won had they had Fisk on instead of Hockentiall. This is saying rather a lit, but the run of the play showed that it was only Warrington's lack of scoring power on the left wing that lost them the game. Elocklnh al did not play atiall badly, but he is not quite in the same class as Fish, and missed scoring one try that the latter would have jumped at. Another mark has been put opposite Swinton's name and they are going to get their deserts next Saturday, when they come to Warrington.

Excellent weather prevailed, and beyond a fairly strong breeze everything should have been on the side of a fast, open game. But for some reason or other the Swinton officials have got their ground covered to a depth of abut three inches with oat husks. If there is anything the Warrington men detest it is having to play in this stuff, and in the cup-tie at Boughton a year or two ago, they insisted on it being cleared away. lam surprised at the Swinton players putting up with it, for it is no end of a nuisance to speedy players. As BDSCOW remarked it was like playing in a farmyard more than on a football field. The ball failed to bounce whenever it dropped and the consequence was rather to Warring- ton's disadvantage—they are so fond of watching a ball bounce. However they made the best of matters and did not do it at all badly.

The first few minutes of play were enough to upset them, for the Swinton flier, Lewis, had an imaginary vision of the Booth Hall Plate and raced over the line in a most absurd fashion—from a Warrington point of view. He didn't get the plate, but he got the try all right and there was some lusty shouting. They seem to think ratter a lot of the plate-winner at Swinton and make tho little mistake of cheering frantically when- ever the bill comes within his scope of vision, let alone reach. Of course this premature jollification does no harm to anybody but the jollifiers—office dictionary lost !—and Lewis is a smart thre equarter.

To resume, however, after Lewis had put the ball between the sticks, Goodman failed to kick a goal and this seemed to have more effect on Warrington than the try had. They" tucked up" as the man in the street says, and things soba bectrne sultry about the den of lions. Winning forward, Warrington kept ap a hot attack,and presently they were rewarded br their exer- tions ny a try scored in pretty fashion by Nierwood. With both sides level play waged furiously, but the visi- tors msre than held their own, and the score wal unal- tered at half time. The swond half opened in similar fashion, but fortune smiled on the Lions. Duckworth passed when he should not have done, with the result that Hampson intercepted and was speeding gayly for the line when the mistake was discovered. He got over all tight though Boscow made a big effort to meet him in the matter. With their noses once more in front the Lions went in for blocking Warrington's movements,and play deteriorated somewhat towards the close. Warrington's last chance had gone, and they had finally to accept defeat by 6 points to 3 points.

Warrington's principal advantage was in the front rank, the footwork and heeling-out of the forwards being much sup,rior to that of the home eight. Boscow was better than Goodman, who appears to labour under the impression that lee is A. J. Gould and Bancroft com- bined. Swinton had some superiority in half and thrce- quarter combination, but this was quite nullified by the robust tackling of the Warrington men. Taylor was the weak spot in the Swinton line,Hampson and Lewis being the pick. " Dai" Davies is over-rated if Saturday's was considered one of his good displays. Morgan played to far more purpose. By the way,there has been a wonder- ful improvement in Allen's play of late. He only needs to pass oftener and more judiciously to be well worth his place. When Fish and Harris are in good trim again the team will be a difficult one to beat.

The Lancashire Senior Co mpetition table up to date is as Icelow. Runcorn strengthened their position by a meritorious win at Brought on. Warrington have now seven clubs above them, and will have to make certain of all the points possible or the record will be inferior to last year's. Fifteen points out of sixteen matches is very unsatisfactory indeed. Leigh, Widnes ,and Salford are not far ahead. however, and ought to lm and must be passed.
The League table up-to-date is as follows :

The Hull match was one of the meat interesting foot• ball displays seem on the Warrington ground, and the success of the home team was gained by sheer merit. Hull were fairly well represented—better so than when they beat Warrington at Hull—and they played a good game. But the Warrington backs were irresistible, and the way they combined was a revelation to everybody. Generally their passing is ineffective,but OR Monday the ball was sent along with a rapidity and accuracy that spelt danger every time. AU three tries were the result of concerted movements between half- backs and threequarters. The Hull men freely admitted that they had met more than their match, notwithstanding that such shining lights as Driscoll, Ftanks. and Taylor were playing. Why, I wander, can't Warrington play in this style oftener. They did well at Leigh by nothing but combination, and they would have defeated Runcorn and Swinton if the form 131.1811 maintained. Let us hope the good start in the New Year is no flash in the pan.

A feature of the game with Hull was the disola7 at centre of L Smith, the ex-Wigan man. Some of the Warrington folk were disappointed in him against St. Helens, but others who had seen him at Leih and Runcorn, knew more about his cApabilities. He fairly silenced his doubters on Monday, and was quite the best back on the field. The way he fed Jones was a treat ,and the latter's two tries were the result of Smith's good work. Alto- gether the pair were exceedingly dangerous and should score well in the future if they only keep it up. All the home bachs wera in tip-top form, and flockenhall must be complimented on the exce2dingly pretty try he scored after passing,:and repassing with Isherwood. The lattar is improving at passing, Smith's example appearing to be a useful one.

Franks was about the rick of the Hull backs, and the spectators were generally aimiring him when they were not laughing at him. He I.oks just like" Little Tibia." and nobody would dream of him being a footballer. He is a clever nvonikin all the same, his passing and punt- ing being wonderfully good, while he is not averse to " going for "the biggest of his oppenects. Driscoll did very little, while Taylor was often at fault. Consider- able interest was evinced in the right wing man, Who was the famous Yankee sprinter, Keane, the winner of a few Sheffield handicaps. He has the speed but he will never make a footballer, and might as well quit the field for the path at once. 13herwood and Hockenhall were able to make rings round him. .

Warrington ought to get two points to-day, but they have no easy thing on with Tyldesley. The " Bongers " always use their forward weight to advantage,and War- rington will miss Taylor, who has a shoulder requiring rest. The backs must win the game, and I have no doubt they vi ill if Monday's form is shown. Smith is a doubtful starter, however, as an injury received on Monday may keep him out of the field. Harris will fill the vacancy if there ia one.

Burgess, of Flixten, will turn out with the" A "team to-day. He is considerei a promising player and had a lot to do with Flixtem's win at Warrington. Salford are reported to be chag,rirted at Warrington's capture. I,llly, the Widnes White Rose half back, is receiving further trial.

E&RLESTOWN ROVERS V WIDNES Vtcs.—This match was played at Eirlestown bet3re a fair gate. The Rovers held the upper hand the whole of the game and eventually ran out easy winners by four goals to nil. LANCASHIRE ALLIANCE.

WARRINGTON V. SOUTELPORT EIIGII PARIC.-.-Ikt War- rington. t3outhport started, and Murray gaining pos- session passed to Connor, who ccored an easy goal for VVarrington. B,th teams afterwards attacked in turn, and S )utOport being penaliieJ, Murray rushed the second goat through from a pass by Connor. In the second half bhe visitors attacked frequently, but shot wide. Warrington twice broke away, ad Sanders kicked two goals. Final score :—Warzington, six goals; Southport, none.
LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. Earlestown v. Haydock.

These old local rivele met to play the return fixture under the auspices of the Lanca.snire League on te e Mesnes Groand on New Year's Day. It will be remem- bered that the first match played on Christmas Day at Haydock resulted in a capital win for Earlestown by three goals to none. The visitors brought their full team, bet Earlestown were short' of Whitehouse and this necessitated Heyes going inside right and Flannaean taking his place at right full back. The advertised time for the kick-off was 2.30, but it was nearer 3 0 o'clock when the teams lined up a follows : Earlestown : Chew, goal; Flannagan and Cottam, backs; Peenington, Green and Johnson, half-backs ; Sampson, Heyes, Linton, Leach and Settle, forwards. Haydock : Jee Lc?.P, goal; Aetbury and John Lee, backs ; Raynor, Forshaw and Gaskell,half-backs; Mayor, Surener, Roberts, Fielding, and Harrison, forwards. The vie Ors won the toss and they took advantage of the slight breeze that was blowing, Linton setting the ball in motion on behalf of Earlestown before about 3,000 spectators. Tne leather was taken Ftraight from the centre into the Haydock goal mouth but a huge kick by Ast bury trensf erred the venue ana an exciting melee in the home goal ensued The 1)111 bobbed about in front of Chew in aggravating fashion Mayor eventually relieving the pressure by shooting yards to Lee. A fool against Green was the means of Haydock renewing the attack and Chew was eiven several warm handfuls, all of which were safely negotiated. A sudden burst on the part of the Earlestown forwards took play to the other end where Hes es put in a splendie shot from long range, the ball being met by Leach, as Lee threw it out, and tanged in again, the cautedian this time kicking the ball up the field. Toe home- eters were back again in a trice and Linton cleverly obtaining poisession he raced away and found himself with an open goal. He dribbled the ball near to Lee and tied reads il3 mistake, crashing the ball into the corner of the net at a terrific speed, the custodian having no possible chance of saving. Roused by this reverse the visitors took up the running, and Sumner was left with no one to piss but Chew, but los- ing cmemanti of the ball, he knocked it into the net with his hand, the point being of course, disallowed. \A spell of midfielsi play followed for a while, and then the proceedings were enlivened by some pretty passing between the visitors' front rank, the result of which was that Fielding got in a fine centre, which was met and promptly put *lto the net by Sumner. From vow to the interval both elevens went at it ding-dong, but neither defence was given much trouble- When the whistle blew, the score was one* each Resuming, in the first tow minutes of the second half, the Hayeleck goal had a narrow escape. The ball was dribbled up the field by Settle and passed to Leach.who banged the leather bard and straight at Lee. the cus- todian, almost causing the downfall of his citadel by fumbling with the ball, only just throwing it clear as he was bundled over the line. At this point Hayes went back to his proper position as right back,and Flannagan went left half back, whilst Joheson partnered Sampson on the eght wing. These changes naturally otrengtheued the detence, but the attacking force was weakened in comparison, as Johnson was really not fit to have played, his leg being swathed in bandages. To make matters worse Green got injured and had to retire, but he came tack again after about ten minutes rest. As the end appreached both teams strove hard to gain the winning paint, but in vain and the whistle eventually blew with the score: Earlestown, one; Haydock, one. The game was hy no nes ans what might be ex- pected from such old rivals and as is generally the case when these clubs meet, a great deal of feeling was in- troduced into the play, and as a consequence fouls were very freqaont. Earlestown ought to be well satisfied at the result of the two matches at least as far as points go as Stalvbridge Rovers are the only team who have taken three points out of Haydock.

div.head: -•-e,..- WATCHNIGHT SERVICES.
div.p: -•-e,..- WATCHNIGHT SERVICES.
Bold-street Wesleyan Church.

In accordance with the usual custom, watchnight sEr- vices were held at most of the places of worship in War- rington on Sunday evening. In some instances there were large congregations, appropriate sermons beiael preached with reference Co the war. The dawn of the New Year was made known by the ringing of Church bells, and by the sounding of the" buzzers" at many of the works. The streets were filled with people for a couple of hours after midnight. ' Tnere was a goad congregation at Bold-street Wesleyan Church, the preacher being the Rev. Theodore Bishop, superintendent of the circuit, who took for the subject of his discourse the words" The end of all things is at band." During the course of his remarks he said that the old proverb, " The end crowns the work " contained a great deal of truth. Life was like a building,and they were the workers with the materials all round them. The scaffEeding might hide the outline and the perfection of the architecture, but when it was taken down, when all the hoardings had been removed, then the edifice stood in all its beauty. Life was very much like that. They were the builders, they had the material all around them, each day opportunities were afforded them, and each day brought to them s maothing that they could use, and if teey were wise use well, in order to make a perfect building. But builders materials were not beautiful, bricks were not beautileal taken singly, nor lime, nor mortar, but when placed together by skilful hands a erand structure was the re- sult and showed the genius of the architect. Life was also like a statue. A block was placed before the artist, the ideal was in his brain, and his b hands worked at it until at last he made it to stand before them in all its wonderful perfection. It seemed to him that God's providence was like the sharp chisel of the sculptor. If they wbuld persevere then God would help to make them better Christians. God's design in their life was that they could all prepare for eternity. Life to the child jut finishing his work at the day school had only begun, and they as parents should try to tell the child that his life at school was only a preparation. Life, with all its joys, care's; sorrows and difficulties was oely lik,t being at school. 'They were on the earth for a short time, when they had spent this life in earnest—the lite " which knows no ending." There were only two ways of leading that life—one good and the other bad, one heaven and the other hell. There was no inter- mediate place, it was either one or the other, and it was their duty to prepare their lives accordingly. They could make their lives successful or spoil them by care- lessness, by delay and by deliberate sin. The text said "The end of all things is at hand." Since St. Peter wrote that centuries had passed by. He thought it was near at hand, and there were never wanting men who thought the same. The end of the world had baen prophesied times ;eithout number by these men, and they had given the actual dates, but it went on and every day that passed bieught them nearer to the end, as far las they were concerned. Their work was to prepare for it whenever it came. Some people led very reckless lives, uncultivated lives, and there was nothing left but a few weeds. It was a standing reproach. Why did they not make this life productive ? It was wickedness not to use their lives to benefit themselves and others. The old prcverb said " There's a tide in the affairs of man, which taken at the flood leads on to fortune." There was a great deal of truth in that. Putting it spiritually, there was an opportunity given to all men which led to fortune, not a fortune of gold, but an op- portunity of giving their services to God—soul and spirit, a living sacrifi^e It would result in a fortune that would last all through eternity.—A collection was taken on behalf of orphans and outcasts.

UTILIZING ME WoLF.—His faithful wife strove to comfort the starving humourist. "Take heart," she urged, "and write." He gazed at the bire, cheerless walls and fireless hearth. "I cannot," he murmured. "Even now the wolf is at the door !" With the words a sudden inspiratien darted into his face. Grasping an axe, he crawled through a cellar window and fell upon the animal from behind. That night the humourist, after tho first steak dinner he had eaten for weeks, wrote eighty-eight wolf jokes. ESTABLISHING AN ACQUAINTANCE. A little Irishman smoking a short clay pipe entered a crowded public-house, walked up to the her, elbowed several customers aside, took a mato from the match-stand on the counter, lit his pipe, and then walked out without a word. The astonished barman gazed after him in amazement and audibly wondered who he was. The very next morning the Irishman walked into the same place, made his way to the counter, lit his black pipe, and started out again. As the little man reached the door, the barman recovered his voice suffi- ciently to call out: "I say! who are yon?" The Irishman turned round and said "You know me." Then he walked out. The barman said that he would lie in wait for the intruder the next day. At about the same hour he reappeared, helped him- self to a match as usual, and lit his short pipe. He was about to turn away, when someone grabbed him by the !Appel of his coat. "Who are you, flow?" dernanded the barman. "Oh, you know me," replitt I,e little Irishman. "No, I don't," said the man :I', the white apron. " Who are you?" "Why,' the cool reply, "I'm the man that comes in ha,a :a light his poipe ivory marnin'."

= A WORRIED WO3IAN.—" Oh, dear," sighed Mrs. Junius, shaking her head. "I wish I could make up my mind what to do with that old green dress of mine. Here I've been thinking over it day and night for a week, and I declare I'm more muddled than when I began." Mr. Junius stirred medita- tively with his spoon. "Your mind," he said, "is like this coffee." "I'd like to know, Julius, what you mean by that," cried his wife, staying the piece of meat half-way to her lip?, "if indeed there's any meaning to it at all which generally I'm sure there isn't and especially comparing your wife to things to drink is something no true gentleman would be guilty of nor would I have ever married you it 1 had supposed I was going to be insulted at my own table for well you know it is and bought with money I ,saved by not doing the washing at a laundry where they charge double not to mention blueing in. the shirt bosoms making them streaked and you laying the blame on to me like every man who has a patient wife. Oh yes, Julius, that's all very well for you to sit there grinning like a graven image at that napkin-ring but far more decent would it be for you to own up to some of the help you get from me slaving friy finger tips away at home with you . spending your money on your cheap companions in town and thinking up things to say about your wife's mind and then all at you laughing at the poor faithful women wearing out their lives and aprons washing dishes and turning dresses like this green one of mine so that our husbands can hays new overcoats while we go along the streets all ,winter having people who are rich pointing the .finger of scorn at us and you caring no more than the wind that blows about eNciting my curiosity

over your foolish conundrums else if you did why would you sit there so dumb Julius winkin,, at that plate of toast with inc caring not the least thing about it except your aggravating way of not explaining why it is that my mind is like that codes." Mrs. Junius, here remembering the piece O[ mert on her fork, stopped her mouth with it, and her husband seized the advantage. "Your mini is like this coffee," he said, directing another conte,nplative glance into his cup, "because it is so dreadfully unsettled." And above the dull rumbling of a passing furniture van Mr. Junius could cleo.rly discern the comments of his—er— better 114 i.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON

LOCAL MUSICAL SUCCESS. At the Musical Bisteddfud held in connection with the Liverpool Sunday School Union, Miss Lottie Jones of the Baptist Sunday School, Earles- town and a pupil of Mrs.Latimer, A R.C.O.,obtained second prize tor solo singing in the class tor teachers or scholars.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD. The death has been reported to the police at Earlestown of Arthur Worsley, 19 weeks old, son of Arthur Worsley, boilermaker, ot 51., Clarence-street, Newton Common, which took place on December 31st. The deceased child had been suffering from whooping cough for about a fortnight, and on the 31st had a severe attack of coughing, and became black in the face. About 11 pm. the mother went to bed with the child, and about one o'clock in the morning it awoke, and was fed, afterwards fall- ing asleep again. About eight o'clock next morning when the mother awoke she found the child lying on her arm dead. The facts were reported to the Coroner, but he did not consider an inquest necessary.
NEW YEAR'S DAY AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

A damp, cold morning, with more than a suffi- ciency of fog heralded the advent of the New Year, but this did not deter a very large number of people from taking advantage of the holiday to spend a day with their friends, and to enjy them- selves in other ways, On New Year's eve, watch night services were held at all the places of wor- ship, and were exceptionally well attended. As midnight struck, there were numerous ascents of rockets accompanied by the blowing of steam whistles, whilst on every hand could be heard the banging of knockers, and the familiar "A happy New Year." The only attraction in the town on New Year's day was the football much between Earlestown and Haydock, which attracted about 3,000 people. In the evening the various tea parties and entertainments were held at the different Sun- day schools, an account of which will be found else- where. At the Viaduct and Vulcan Works,business was resumed on Tuesday morning, but at Messrs. Vicars' and Slees the men did uct tun in until Wednesday morning, NEWTON OUNG MEN'S BIBLE CLASS.

A social evening in connectim with tl,e aline was held in the Town Hail, Newton-le-Willaws on New Years' Day, about 120 being present. The room had been tastefully decorated by Alh?8 Sankey and a number of assistants. A splendid programme of dancing was provided, The Vicar in a short address, said he was pleased to see so many there and hoped they would have a prosperou;, New Year. It had been said that dancing was not the thing for such assemblies,but heithougb t that dancing was one of the best and purest amusements We have in the country. Songs were rendered between the dances by the Misses Wilkinson and Gorse and Messrs J Mather, Bartlett,ll Houghton, T Braddock and B Grace, and a recitation by Mr Lane. The non- dancers were well provided with games and nothing was left undone, to provide a pleasant evening. Mr Wilkinson proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies for their kindness in providing the refresh- ments, etc, which was carried unanimously. Mr Singleton replied on their behalf and said that they were indebted to Mr J H Lane, the secretary for the energetic way in which be had worked t. make the affair a success. Mr Laze suitably repliea and also , proposed a vote of thanks to the pianist, Miss lßodmer, which was heartily accorded

div.head: NEW YEAR ENTERTAINMENTS AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON,
div.p: NEW YEAR ENTERTAINMENTS AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON,
BAPTIST SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The annual tea and entertainment in connection with the above was held in the schoolrooni, Earlestown on Monday. The tea was served about half past four,about ' 150 children and adults being present. The tables wee presided over by the teachers and the tea was much en- joyed. The subs t quent proceediegs were presided over by the Rev F E Me:er. The Secretary Mr W Limond in presenting his annual report said—" In reviewing the pat twelve months' work in connection with our school I think we have every reason to be thankful for what we have achieved and for the steady pregress we are making. Numerically we are I fear not making the pro- gress we would like to make, at the same time our average attendauce is better than in former years, the young men especially showing up better ; the number of scholars on the books is 190, and teachers 28. Our finances as tpuel give us no cause for alarm and in this respect I cannot but refer to the anniversary collection last May. when we raised the grand sum of £43 19s ; to which a further sum of £1 is Od was added, making a total of £45. I need hardly say tint the best thanks of the :teachers and officers are tendered to those who assisted on that eccasion both pecuniarily and otherwise,and in order to show that we still have your sympathy let us see if we cannot raise £5O at our anniversary next May. The re- wards to he given this evening number 74 presentsd by the schoel for attendance; conduct, and repeating the text, and 10 other books given by Mrs. Valentine. Those of you who were present at our last distribution will doubtless remember that Mrs. Valentine offered to give a reward to the most deserving scholar. The teachers had several talks over the matter and subject, to the approval of Mrs Valentine, decided that the most deserving scholar was the one who attended every ser- vice held in the school during the year, the result being that 10 scholars (9 girls and 1 boy), have qualified for the prize —Mrs Valentine has, however, kindly offered to give a book to each scholar, so that the difficulty of selecting the most deserving has been avoided. The entertainment consisted of lantern views, recita- tions, solos, dusts, and dialogues, in which the children took part. During the evening the awards to the scholars were distributed by Mrs Valentine and Mrs Miller. Certificates from the Liverpcol Sunday School Union Eiteddfeel were presented to Miss Lottie Jones who gained 2nd prize for solo singing, Mr S Harvey, 3rd prize for musical composition, and Mr W Limond Ist prize for solo singing.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODISTS.
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODISTS.

A to% and social were he!d in connection with the Primitive Methodist Christian Endeavour. About 80 were present to tea, the honours of the tahle being per- formed by the female memters of the Society. After tea the evening was enjoyably spent in gemes of vari..us kinde.

div.head: NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL.
div.p: NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL.

The annual scholars tea and entertainment was held in the schoolroom. About 150 sat down to tea, over which the teachers presided. The Rev. James Allatt presided over the subsequent proceedings and after ex- tending a welcome to all present, briefly referred to the work of the past year. The Ageistant Secretary, Mr. D. McHardy, submitted a report oa the affairs of the school uring the year past endel. The entertainment consisted of part songs, action songs, duets, dialogues, and solos, the programme being sustained by the scholars under the conductorship of Mr. A. Knight. A dialoeue "Circumstantial Evidence" was very well submitted, the characters being upheld by elder scholars.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S CHURCH.

The annual social lathering of the Young Men's Bible Class in connection with St. John's Church was held in the Mission Hall. There were about 150 to tea which wan touch enjoyed. After tea dancing was indulged in acd spiritedly carried on to music supplied by Mr Lewis. The Dif.C'e. were Mresrs. Ha.rdman end Garnet and dancing was kept up until 12 o'clock. EABLESTOWN WESLEYANS.

This year the Wesleyans departed from their usua custom of a tea party, and gave only an entertainment. The Rev. Mr. Passmore presided, and there was a very large attendance. An interesting ddress was given by the Rev. Beng, Weaver, and a number of songs, &c., were rendered by members of the choir and others.—The Secretary. Mr. T. Parr, in presenting the 45th annual report of the Sunday School observed that the ministry of the Church was a proof of the influence of Sunday schools, and of their own school they could not be other- wise than gratified at having supplied a few of her trained nsinisters. They welcomed in their midst that day an old scholar and teacher of the school. whose prestos gave them an opportunity of reflecting upon the lalstory of the school. They felt very thankful to all their friends and sup- porters for the very literal response to their appeals. for financial aid, and as will be naturally supposed the expenses in carrying on such a large school must be heavy. But though their expenses were htavy 'hey were pleased to report a small balance in hand. The school was divided into three sections, viz., seniors, juniors and infants, these were further divided lot:) 31 classes. The number of teachers and officers on the boots was 70. Average attendance of teachers and officers, morn- ing 16.33. afternoon 28.46. Numter of scholars on the book. 520 Average attendance. morning 138.78 after- noon 303 'l9. They asked for the co-operation of the parenis in seeing, that their children attend more regul- arly, csoecially on Sunday morning.and then they would have every reason to hope for a better average atten- dance this year. The Juvenile Missionary Association Still cantinues to do its important work in connection with the school. The Bind of Hope Society was still an active one in connection with the school. The number of members enrolled for this par was 140. With regard to the school finances the net income from el sources was £6B is lid, and expenditure £62 13s lid,leaving a balance of £5 83 9id (Applause.) During the evening a number of books were dis- tributed to the scholars as prizes for regular attendance during the year.

He adopts this course, having received so many letters con...plainin.T that Beecham's Pills cannot at pre- sent be obtained at the front.

LETTER FROM MR. FRANK REYNOLDS. "General Buller the right man in the right place." The following interesting letter has been received by Mrs. S. Reynolds,from her nephew Mr. Frank Reynolds: —Elandslaagte Collieries, Limited, 32e, Smith-street, Durban, December 7th, 1899. My dear aunt,—l hope the mail after this will carry long letters from Guy. I hope the day is not far sissy when we shall hear that Ladysmith has been relieved. They have had a long time there and will be very glad to have some news of the outside world. We hear that a forward move is ex- pected any day, and General Buller has a large body of men under his command. He is the right man in the right place. Colonists hive perfect confidence in him. A move that he has made since he came is ore that, ought to have been made at the first, and that is the raising of as many mounted men as poseibie. Hundrees of mounted colonists are now going forward- Time after time have the colonists asked to be allowed to, raise corps and do what they can to assist in defendine. ' the co'ony against the Boers, but for some reason the military authorities have thrown cold water on it. Now Buller has cem i he not only encouraged it but is doing all he can to make it in every way a success. These colonist scouts as they are called will be able to keep the Boers togsther instead of allowing them to roam all over the ceone, looting farmers' stock and destroying everything. If the Boere want to fight let them keep together where our soldiers can find them. I hope when this reaches you that the worst of the fighting will be over, and theh, let us hope, peace will soon come over the land once more. But on no account must the Beers, be allowed to rule in South Africa again. England and her colonies have paid in blood and money for their rights and so let us hope she will stick to them. A firm hand for a few yea--s and then the Englieh flag will be safe through- out South Africa for ever. I hope Christmes will be a happy one for you and I hope I may have the pleasure of seeing Goy before that day. As soon as I can get to Ladysmith I am going up. —Eloping the New Year will bring you her fair share of blessings, your affectionate nephew, FRANK REYNOLDS. It should be mentioned that Mr. Reynolds is a native of Natal. Mrs. Reynolds received on December 26th the following telegram, sent on Christmas Day :—" Well, Guy, Ladysmith." DEPARTURE OF WARRINGTON ' RESERVISTS. An enthusiastic " send-off" was accorded Constables Gibbs and Ilesp of the boroui. h police force, who journeyed by the 9.30 train from the Central Station on Saturday morning to rejoin their regiment the Grenadier Guards at Wellington Barracks. A large etowd of friends, including members of the force lassembled on the platiOrm aud several affecting scenes were witntesed The train left at ten o'clock and needless to ta heer ae ?r cheer was raised as it steamed out of t eta. on. P.C. Bradley, who had elo rec-iived order to rejoin the Grenadier Guards loft Ban; Quay S ei.tion by the 11.27 train en, route for Wellington Barracks, his wife and family and a good numb rof friends being present. We understand that P.O 's Gibbe and Bade have been allowed a month's furlough and well in tee meantime resume their dutiee P.C. Heel) has been disqualified as medically unfit. Thomas Fell, a reservist of the Royal Engineers and an employee cf Messrs. Mackie and Ca, Limited, loft Bank Quay Stitiou on Saturday tee• tee helequarters of his regiment. Ho had a hearty send-efT i'rons his workmates ard the " Guardian " Band enlivened the proceedings with several selections. George Sant, a carter, in the employ of the Warring- ton Slate Company, also had a very enthusiastic send-off. He left the Central etation amidst the che2rs of a large crowd of his feline workmen about three o'clock on Saturday afternoorefor Ashtor-under-Lyne. to rejoin the 2nd Battalion Manchester Regiment.

div.head: RESERVIST IN TROUBLE AT WARRINGTON.-ASSAULT ON A RAILWAY INSPECTOR.
div.p: RESERVIST IN TROUBLE AT WARRING- TON.-ASSAULT ON A RAILWAY INSPECTOR.

On Monday, at the Borough Police Court, before Mr. Birchall (in the chair), Councillor Smethurst and Mr. S. Wright, John George Barbour, a young man, was charged with having been drunk at Bank Qty Station on Saturday afternoon, making use of obscene languaze, and as3aulting Inspector Liarsley.—Detective Howells appeared on behalf of the railway company. He said that the prisoner arrived at the station at 2.30 and askt d for a platform ticket, which was given to him for the high level platform. as he wished to see the reservists oil. Ile was noticed to be under the influence of drink. , When the ticket was given to him by Ticket- collector Blinston he doubled it up, made use ci disgusting language, and rushed off to the phi:- form. There were trany ladies and gentlemen about at the time, and they complained of the disorderly conduct of the prisoner. When Harbour returned to the platform he went to Inspector Efarsley and said he would like to " do something for him," and eventually struck him in the face with hie fists* The men closed and strugglsd on tbn floor, and when aesit.tance was obtained the prisoner was given into custody. fie was very violent and struck at all who came near him. It was with great difficulty that the handcuffs were put upon him The man bad rendered himself liable to a penalty of 403., but the London and Nnrh-Western RAlway Company did not wish ta unduly press tat) ease. lie understood that the prisoner was a reservist, and had been in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee as a constable at their waggon works at Warrington for about three years. From the papers which had been found in his possession he ought to have presented him- self at tha Barracks on Saturday.—Evidence in support lof the above statement having been Eiven,—Prisoner said he was very sorry to hear what had been said about him, but he was drunk on Saturday and did not re- member what took place. This was his first appearance in a police court, and he hoped, therefore, that the Bench would be lenient with him—The Chairman : It is a terrible thing to find a man who is supposed to act in the interests of order in such a position.—Councillor Smethurst : This is the first day of the year, and had the case not been a serious one, We should have felt di,- posed to let the man off.— The Chairman said the London and North-Western Railway Company's servants must Ibe protected from the conduct of 'non in the habit of getting foolishly drunk. Tne prisoner would be fined 103.

Ashtnal (clerk.)—The Clerk :tenoned the receipt of a telegram from the Inspector of Nuisances, sa yiog that he should not attensi the melting unless he (the Clerk) requested him to do so.—The Chairman inquired whether it was the duty of the Inspector and the Snrveyor to attend the meetings ; if not the committee had no power over them.—The Clerk considered that it was just as much their duty to attend as any other offisial.—Ar. Williams : The proper way to settle this matter will be to have it discuised at the District Council tneethig, as it is absolutely impossible to do the work of the committee with any degree of satisfaction without the attendance of the Inspector and Stirveyor.—The Clerk read a letter from the Loco! ' IG,Jverument Beard, enclosing model of 'amended bylaws i for Frodshani, m whth it was stated that the Board, as at present advised, would not he prepared to san,Ai the width of ten feet as a minimum for secon- dary means of access. Streets of an unlimited length should he of a width of 16 feet at the !amt. Ibut they had added a provision to the clause wh'ch would permit such streets under certain conditiens to be twelve feet in wicith.—lt was resolved that the n-;odel bylaws as amended by the Local Government Board be adopted.—The collector of the water rates reported that the rate levied for the qaarter :amounted to £147 3s 51. and that the .errers brought forward were £34 5; 51, making £lBl 8 10,1, and of this sum £134 14s 4cl hid been collected, having arrears of £46 13s 63. Prior to rising, the chairolan wished the Councillors " A Happy New Year," and hoped that the meetings in the future would be as pleasant a; they had been during the past year. Mr. Kycld, on behalf of his fellow coonciilor,3, tbalik :ii the Chairmen for his kind expressions.
Judge Wynne Ffoulkes' Successor.

- - The Registrar of the Warrington County Court has received a communicatim from Sir K.-nneth Muir Mackenzie to the effect that the Lord Chancel- lor has appointed as Judge Wynne Ffoulkes' succes- sor Mr A Gw)nne James, 2, Temple-gardens, Temple, EC., as judge of the county court on Cir- cuit No. 7. The circuit comprises Warrington, Northwich, Wiusford, Altrincbarn, Runc-ern an,l Birkenhead. Mr. Gwyone James is a nephew of Lord James, and son of Mr. Gwynne James, a well- known solicitor of Hereford, of which city the new judge is R-,corder. Mr. James was educated at Cheltenham and Trinity College, Cambridge, and after winning one of the studentships was called to the Bar at Middle Temple in 1881,and joined the- Oxford circuit,where for some years past he has en joyerl a substantial practice. lie has the reputation at the Bar of being a sound lawyer and a man of great sagacity, as well as kindly and courteous in manner. He is 43 years of age and unmarried. The impression amongst those who know him is that he will prove an admirable County Court judge. ROBLEY WATER SUPPLY.

The Local Government Board wrote directing atten• tion to the remarks on page 48 of the annual report for 1898 of the Medical Officer of Health, with reference to the need of an improved water supply for N3rley. and inquiring what action had since been taken by the Coun- cil to provide a proper supply for that place. Mr. S Woodward observed that toe representative for Norley not being present, he, as representative of the adjoining parish, might bay he had reisia to kuow that certain circumstances had arisen in the township which made it impossible for any large scheme to he contem- plated. There had been a change in property owners and one change upon one estate alone was sufficient to complicate matters. He thought, however, in the im- mediate future the heal council at Norley would give the matter full consideration. He (Mr. Woodward) did not agree with the recommendation of the Medical Officer to secure a water supply from the Liverpool source, but thought there was a very good source oi water in Norhy which might be utilised in a sheme of their own. He movei moat the letter be forwarded to the Norley Parish Council. Mr. C E Lnker seconded,and the motion was agreed to.

THE LIVERPOOL CORPORATION AND TUBERCULOSIS..

Mr. C. E Linker called atteqion to a newspwer re- port of intention of the Liverpool Corporation ap, plying for an Act of Pa,rlilm.tut that would affect the milk purveyors in their (th District Council's) country districts, and proposed that the Clerk be empowered to obtain a copy of the proposed Bill for the consideration of their Parliamentary Committee. RIVERS' POLLITTION.—A MOVE. Mr. J. Mclntyre submitted the reporc of the Rivers' Pollution Committee, from •Nhich ir; would appear the commit.tee hal caused 14 effi lents to be analysed. Ten of them would not require immediate attention. Of the remaining fi,ur : two had been taken in hand by the County Council; and the Rivers' Pollution Committee re- commended that the other two should be referred to the Parish Councils wi,hin whose districts they were, for their consideration, as they had reason to believe that a solution may be found for them. He seconded tho adoption of the report which was carried unanimously.

div.head: CANAL BOATS ACTS.
div.p: THE CANAL BOATS ACTS.

In compliance with -the pr-ovision of the Canal Boats Acts, 1877 and 1884, Mr. James Farrington submitted his repor; :—" Tho inspoction of Canal Boats is under- taken by the Inspector of Nuisances along with his other duties ; his remuneration of the same being £lO per annum."—Twentv-aeven boats were inspected, which owing to the illness of the Inspector was much smaller than that for the previous year.—The condition of the boats and their occupants were found to be quite satis- factory. The report was considered satisfactory.

div.head: RUNCORN TECHNICAL INSTITUTE
div.p: RUNCORN TECHNICAL INSTITUTE
Students Social.

aThrough the kind invitation of the Runcorn Technical Instruction Committee the students at the day and evening classes to the number of about 160 with a few friends held their annual social at the Institute,Waterloo- road,en Wednesday evening. The place, and especially the new wing, had been most tastefully decorated with flsge Chinese lanterns and bunting and presented quite an enlivened appearance when the students and their friends began to arrive. Amongst those present we noticed Mr F Wiswall (chairman of the Urban District Council). Mrs, Mr and Miss Wiwsll, Mr and We J W Lightbura, Mr and Mrs George Hewitt. Mr J Wilson, Mr J Littler, Mr and Mrs J H Weston, Mr and Mrs E Marshall, Mr and Mrs George Bellamy, Mr James:and Miss Wilding, Mr and Mrs A Lightburn, Mr W E Dudley (chairman of the Runcorn Co-operative Society). Mr and Mrs J D Jones (libarian), Mr aud Mrs W Jones, Mr W Hankinson, Mr Lawrensen (hea,imaster), Mr Hutchings, (art master), Mr and Mrs J Speakman, Mr F W Butt(in, Mr 11 Chadwiek,Miss Dukes, Mr J M Frith, Mr C Handley, Mr F Austin and Mr W floward.—The preceedings opened with an exhi- bition of the students' work which was admirably set out in the art room, where were visible many interesting specimens in colour' black and white, and applied art, clay modelling, woodwork, and building construction. Mr. J H Hutchings (art master) was to be seen there, also, exhibiting to an admiring greup the method of manipulating the potter's wheel. Then fol- lowed an amateur theatrical performance in the new wing by members of the Lyric Amateur Theatrical Company" (Liverpool), which proved highly amusing. The scenery was kindly lent by Mr. Caddie, lessee of the Runcorn Theatre.—Upitairs another side show wag provided by Mr. Booth in exhibitions of Gramaphone records.—&n ample and substantial retresh- tnent hat was in coaree of Mr. W. Spearing—After the corpthuion of the theatrics! tnte tainmect the lecture room of the Necv Win:z was cleared for a" Cinderella," music being previdei by Mr. Ravenserof.—On the whele the evenine proved enjoyable, but at times the proc ,edings s:eowod a tendency to drag.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. THE ATTACK ON COLESBERG.

div.head: Boers Surrounded.
div.p: Boers Surrounded.
FIGHTING INCESSANT.
Rensburg, Wednesday, 5.20 p.m.—The Boers at Coles- berg are almost surrounded, but stiil keeping us out of the town.
Fighting is incessant in the hills. Our artillery force the enemy to keep themselves care- fully concealed.
BIG DEVELOPMENTS EXPECTED.
A Naauwpoort telegram says : We command Norval's Pont with two guns, also Colesberg Bridge. The Boers have no way of retreat except by Norberg. A big development is expected to-morrow.
Boer attack Repulsed at Mo Reno, From General Cape Town to Secretary of State for War.

Cape Town, January 3.—Referring to my telegram of January 1 (1) learn Dordrecht now evacuated by Mont- morency, who has occupied Bird's Siding. Indove line. Molten° to-day is being attacked by the enemy, who more or less surround police station, but who, by latest reports, are being forced back. Reinforcements of mounted infantry have been sent by Gateacre, as well as half a battalion by train to Bush- man's Reek, and a battery of Field Artillery, under escort, along the road to thd last place. Result unknown.

div.head: Dash from Ladysmith.
div.p: A Dash from Ladysmith.

Pretoria, Monday (via Loam za Marques, Wednes- day).—A telq.fram from the Boer head laager loz4ore Ladysmith, dated to-day, says that during a heavy storm four nights ago six horsemen escaped from Lady- smith under cover of the darkness and pierced the Boor lines. They are believed to include Colonel Rhodes and Dr. Jameson.

div.head: METHUEN'S COLUMN.
div.p: METHUEN'S COLUMN.
Guards Wounded,
MODDER RIVER, WEDNESDAY EVENING,

A detachment from the Guards yesterday made a small demonstration in front of the enemy's works on our extreme right. They succeeded in drawing the enemy's -fire. One party approached closer towards a Boer redoubt when a shell burst among them, and three men were wounded.

div.head: SOLDIER WRITES TO HIS RUNCORN
div.p: A SOLDIER WRITES TO HIS RUNCORN
FRIENDS. With the Lancers at Modder River.

Private Edward Allen, of the 12th Lancers, now at the Madder River, writing from that place to Mr W Cobbler, Friendship Arms, Runcorn (a retired member of the same regiment) says : " Dear friend, I receivtd your very welcome letter, and was pleased to hear you were all in good health, for myself I am in splendid condition. Beer is not to be got for gold. We are kept very busy as they (the Boers) are continually sending out raiding parties. 'Mr y are rank cowards every one of them. A wounded Boer shot a doctor whilst he was dressing his wounds, and another one shot a Sister of Mercy. All the prisoners we capture are all glad, and they give all the information they can without being asked for it. Dirty dogs! My officer—Mr Frisham ? and the whole of my section were lot, except myself and one other. We were lucky te get away. We were reconneitering on the morning of the fifth and were surprised so the right section of number 3 troop is missing, bar two, and we are a-coming up again. 'Twas a h—of a gallop that we got away with. We all swam the river and I am afraid that is where we lost them. I know they are wounded and hope that is all. We have about 12 men wounded besides them. If you keep on the move they can't hit you. lam always scout- ing, and bullets whistle around you like flies buzzing but seldom kill. By keeping at a hard canter you have a good chance. Tne worst of it is when we go out in small parties, they surprise you by coming up all round, then you have to go through them. Our base of operations at present is Mockler River where we now are. Toe Boers lie fan-shaped all round us in the hills, from which we will shift them to-morrow or next day. As this is Sunday we are not doing much, though we are all ready saddled and could be on parade in two minutes ready to clear away. The Medical Staff Corps is making plenty of money from those we leave behind (Boer dead). Unfortunately we have to keep right ahead of the column for chances Cl a charge. They fly like the .D--from a lance point. A squadron can chase any number of them if we can cello get them out of the hills. We—that is "B"—chased 700 of them from Gras Pan where they had a company of the Northum- berland Fusiliers hemmed in. We had to march 16 miles to their relief, and were only just in time as they could not have held out another half-hour. We have a lot of that sort of work. We have been at Victoria West, Do Aar, Orange River, Naupaurt, Bel- mont, Gras Pan, Madder River. Our next move is an attack on Spytfontien, and then on to Kimberley which is 24 miles from here. By the time you get this (letter) it will be old news, though it will be tough work ; and I think that it will be the Boers last stand though they tell you they can last another 12 mouths. I expect this will be a long time reaching you, as yours has been a long time reaching me. You get more news of the war at home than we do • • Then follows a little personal matter Continuing the writer calls his friends" happy men to have good beer to drink, and promises to sEnd a set of whiskers in his next letter. People talke3 of it making you " bob " when under fire—" it'e all rot." I thought no more of it than a field day at Aldershot. The only thing that I can see is the men are all anxious to get in the thick of it. All coma are alike in that resplct. They drop without a murmur. The Brigade of Guards are splendid."—The letter conclud7s with affectionate remembrances.

div.head: WOUNDED WARRINGTON MAN AT THE
div.p: A WOUNDED WARRINGTON MAN AT THE
FRONT.

It is with regret that we notice that Corporal A. Chap- pell, 2nd Liverpool Regiment, who was wounded at Orange River, is amongst the iist of those who are not doing well, being dangerously wounded. Corporal Chappell is the son of Mr. J. B. Cha ppel, of Knutsford- road.
THE THIRD SOUTH LANCASHIRE MILITIA. Mobilisation at Warrington.

On Wednesday morning the Army aticials at Orford Barracks were engaged in the work of mooilisation of the 3rd South Lancashire Prince of Wales's Volunteers (Militia) Regiment,which has received orders to proceed to South Africa on the 11th iest. No pressure was put upon the man to go on active service, anti it is quite optional for them to decline to serve. It is however satisfactory to state that the vast majority volunteered, and very few remained behind of their free will. The medical exemieation has been very strict—quite as strict as it is made for recruits—and no one with any trace of disease has been allowed to go. Four hundred men of the regiment were mobilized about three weeks ago and w ere stationed at Preston. Excellent arrangements had been made for equiiiping the remainder of the men about six hundred in number,who were mobilized on Wednesday. By four o'clock the first contingent bad entrained at Bank Quay Station and departed for Preston. A second batch fellowed at 6.24. They will remain at Preston, where they will be clothed in khaki, until the 11th inst., and will then sail for the front. The officers of the battalion include some well-known local gentlemen. They are Lieutenant-Colonel Ireland-Blackburne, Majors Srnythies, Heath, Hall, and Tarbot ; .Ceptains larson, Eckersley, Skirrow, Edey, and Postlethw aite ; Lieuten- ants Vaughan. Stephens, Gordon Stewart, Catelle, Lyon, and Hanbury, L'eutenant-Colonel Ireland-Black- bourne resides at Hale Hal!, and is a relative to Mr. J. Ireland-Blackburne, who for twelve yens was the re- presentative of Warriegron in Parliament. Lieutenant Lyon is the heir of Mr, Thomas Henry Lyon, of Appleton Hall, near Warrington, a laree land- owner. Captain Marson formerly resided at Hill Cliffe and is a colliery proprietor, as also is Captain Eckersley. Lieutenant Hanbury is the son of Mr Hanbury. M.P. for Preston. Major Smythiee is the adjutant lor the 8-40th Regimental District. The mobilisation aroused groat intereA in the town, as a large proportion of the battalion are Warriugton men. During the whole of the morning a large crowd assem- bled outside Orford Barracks, and there was much en- thusiasm on their depaiture. The first portion numbered 167, and the second portion 118. They were under the command of M4jor Hall, ad were played to the station by the deret band. Afurthcr contingent left Warrington on Thunder morning.

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON
Personal.

The Rev. J. 11. G. Hollingwortb, who has offi- ciated 88 curate of St. Pauls' Church, for eight months, has been instituted to the living of St. Barnabas' Church,Lovely-lane. The cenmony took place at the Palace at Liverpool. Infirmary and Liberal Balls Abandoned.

We understand that the annual ball promoted by the Warrington Liberal Association, and the In- firmary ball" have: been abandoned this year owing to the effect on public sentiment caused by the war in South Africa.
New Year's Day.

The banks in Warrington closed at twelve o'clock on New Year's Day, in accordance with the usual custom. The day was also generally observed as a holiday by shopkeepers and others. Gospel Hall, Forster-street.

On Monday night the Sunday school scholars had their annual treat, nearly 300 sitting down to a free tea, after which a collection was made on behalf of the Ntayor's fund for the soldiers, widows, and orphans, which, addei to what was collected by the scholars carol singing, realized 525. A very pleas ant evening was spent.

Fatal Accident to a Woman. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, conducted anl inquest at the Police Station on Monday afternoon, relative to the death of Fanny Molyneux 68 years of age, who resided at 168, Evelyn-street, Sankey Bridges, which occurred on Friday afternoon under circumstances detailed below. The Coroner stated the facts of the case. He said that deceased had suffered for .a number of years from peralysii, and for seven years had been atten- ded by Dr. Hurray, of Penketh. On Tuesday, the 26th of December, at 10.50 p.m. she fell out of bed and her head came into contact with the fender, inflicting a wound. Assistance was obtained, but deceased became unconscious and died on Friday. Dr. Murray said that the accident was the cause of death.—Ann Molyneux, daughter-in-law of the deceased, said deceased who was a widow re- sided with her at 168, Evelyn-street. She was 68 years of age last birthday. She had suffered from Iparalysis for 23 years, and for seven years had been under the care of Dr. Murray. At 11 o'clock on Tuesday night, Decemb3r the 26th. witness was ilk the kitchen when she heard a noise in the parlour where deceased slept. On going into the room she saw deceased lying on the floor with her feet on the fender. he put her in bed ani summoned assistance, and it was found that she had sustained a wound to her fore- head. she never regained consciousness and died on Friday at five o'cleck in the afternoon.—A verdict of " Accidentel death " W9S returned.

div.head: Toney Felix Bankrupt.
div.p: Toney Felix Bankrupt.

The popular clown, Taney Felix, who some years ago visited Warrington with a circus company has lacome bankrupt. In his ob,ervations on:the matter the Official Receiver, Mr. S Wells Page, says that Mr. Toney Felix until May, 1896, fulfilleo -,Hgage- ments with circus proprietors. He then went into partnership with Mr. George Arundale, and they erected a woodcn structure in Wolverhampton, which with fixtures and furniture cost £470. The whole of the capital for the business was found by Mr. Arundale, and the profits were to be equally divided. They continued the circus until October, 1896. They then removed to Birmingham, and erected and furnished a building there at a cost of xBOO. which Mr. Arundale found. The partnership was dissolved by mutual consent, the bankrupt re- ceiving £2OO ard four circus horses and one pony for his share. The bankrupt states that at this time be had a capital of £570, in addition to the four horses and pony. He then went to Warrington and rented a building, and opened a citcus there until January, 1897. He estimated he lost £220 whilst there. He afterwards went to Rotherham, Wolverhampton, West Bromwich, Stockport and other places, where he opened circuses. He ac- counts for his deficiency as follows :—Excess of assets over liabilities, December 11th, 1898, £270 ; amount received for sale of horses in September .1899, £100: deficiency as per statement of affairs .2370 is 7d; total £740 Is 7d; loss from carry- ing on business since December 11th 1898, £460 is 7d; living expenses of self, wife and three children, .£130; money stolen whilst at Stock- port, £5O; loss upon purchase of building at Stock- port subspquentlN pulled down and sold, £100; total. £740 11 VI.

The articles required aro Socks, Balaclava Caps, and Khaki Jerseys, and ladies are re- quested ti contribute either in kind or in money for the pur- chase of these articles. The price of the Socks is estimated at 100. per pair. The Balaclava Caps can be purchased at is. 9d. each, and the Khaki Jerseys at 4s. 6d. each. Money and Articles my be sent to me at the Town Hall. As it is advisable that the parcels should be despatched be- fore the 10th January, although supplem.ntary packages will be sent, early assistance will be gratefully received. HENRY ROBERTS, Mayor.
